investigations.title: Is the LLM biased toward rare codes, or is it only the base rate?

report.headline: The zero-shot LLMs show no special bias toward rare codes. What they lack is a frequency prior, and that only becomes visible where prevalence is tiny. On the pooled uniform draws (8,000 reports, 2025+2026), each rare code is named falsely about as often as a typical code with 21-100 training reports: mean FPR 2.0-4.5e-4 per code against a median of 5.0e-4 for codes with more than 20 training reports. If every rare code had the median frequent-code FPR, false rare answers would stay near 15,000 a year, no fewer than now. The answer rate of zero-shot coders barely follows training frequency below 100 training reports (Poisson slope -0.07 to 0.11, against 0.65 for the filed codes). So the 1-5 band is over-named 19-44x while its precision is about 1%. Within that flat spread the false answers pile onto a few codes, and the same reports pull the same code in all three LLMs. That is driven by the text, and it repeats from 2025 to 2026. Templates are not the cause: these reports cluster no more than a random draw. The false rare answers are more literal than the filed code (the answered term shares a word with the text 41-66% of the time, the filed term 26-33%) and more often sit in an unrelated branch of the code tree. Retrieval removes the effect by bringing back the frequency prior, but it also drops about half of the right rare answers. To reach 50% precision a rare code would need an FPR near 3e-6, which is 70-150x below what any coder shows on any band. Rare-code labelling at natural proportions is therefore the wrong target. Better targets are a review or screening queue, or a fix for the few attractor codes such as the only 'No Apparent Adverse Event' code and literal name matches.

findings.claim: The loader is correct: it reproduces the known encoder and LLM year counts.
findings.evidence: Encoder 2026: 32 right / 166 false rare a year; 2025: 60 / 1. Uniform accuracy 0.6365 (2026) and 0.7482 (2025). Zero-shot 2026: Qwen 131 / 14,693.4, Gemma 158 / 14,476, Opus 154 / 6,664.7. Retrieval 2026: 79 / 2,733.5, 92 / 2,235.2, 95 / 3,025.6. The uniform draw has 4,000 rows a year (3,974 of them have frequent-code gold); the largest weight is 164.0 (2026) and 189.5 (2025).
findings.reproduce: scratch s1_cache.py, then s2_analysis.py (SANITY line), each via run.sh

findings.claim: Over-naming by band: zero-shot LLMs push answers from the >1000 head into every lower band. The 1-5 band is hit hardest relative to its prevalence, but the 6-20, 21-100 and 101-1000 bands are over-named too. The encoder and the retrieval coders stay near 1 except for a 5-10x ratio on the 1-5 band for retrieval.

Per code, zero-shot names rare codes falsely about as often as mid-frequency codes and less often than frequent ones. The mean FPR is roughly flat from 1-5 to 21-100 and only rises for the high-frequency head. Per-code FPR follows training frequency much less for zero-shot (Spearman 0.41-0.65) than for the encoder and retrieval (0.76-0.78).
findings.evidence: Pooled uniform, mean FPR per code (x1e-4) for bands 1-5 / 6-20 / 21-100 / 101-1000 / >1000: zs_qwen 4.51 / 3.48 / 4.56 / 15.6 / 32.2; zs_gemma 3.86 / 7.94 / 3.20 / 15.5 / 28.9; zs_opus 2.04 / 8.11 / 3.77 / 9.54 / 30.7; rag 0.7-0.8 on the 1-5 band; enc 0.03. Median FPR is 0 for every code in the 1-5 and 6-20 bands, except zs_qwen 1-5 at 1.25e-4; the resolution is 1/8,000. Rare codes ever named falsely: zs 25 / 19 / 17 of 46. Spearman(FPR, training count): enc 0.78, rag 0.76-0.78, zs_qwen 0.41, zs_gemma 0.50, zs_opus 0.65.

findings.claim: Zero-shot answers ignore the frequency prior among codes with 100 or fewer training reports.
findings.evidence: Poisson slope of log(answer count per code) on log(training share), pooled uniform, all known codes / codes with <=100 training reports: filed gold 0.88 / 0.65; enc 0.94 / 0.61; zs_qwen 0.48 / 0.09; zs_gemma 0.49 / -0.07; zs_opus 0.64 / 0.11; rag_qwen 0.90 / 0.35; rag_gemma 0.89 / 0.18; rag_opus 0.93 / 0.12.

findings.claim: Precision implied by band FPR and prevalence: about 1% on the 1-5 band for zero-shot, against 42-50% on the >1000 band. Reaching 50% precision on a rare code would need an FPR of about TPR x prevalence, roughly 3e-6, which is 70-150x below the measured rare-code FPR of zero-shot. It is also below the per-code FPR of every coder in every band.
findings.evidence: 2026 per-code prevalence of the 1-5 band is 9.6e-6 (year-weighted). TPR 0.26 / 0.34 / 0.32 (zs qwen / gemma / opus). Precision at band-mean FPR: zs 0.006 / 0.008 / 0.015; rag 0.021 / 0.025 / 0.021; enc 0.127. On the >1000 band zs reaches 0.42 / 0.47 / 0.50. The 3e-6 target is 0.3 x 9.6e-6, set against measured rare FPR of 2.0-4.5e-4.
findings.reproduce: s2_analysis.py section 2c; the required-FPR step is arithmetic on those numbers

findings.claim: Counterfactual: with the median FPR of frequent codes, false rare answers would remain at roughly 7,600-23,000 a year. That is as many as, or more than, the observed counts. The excess is therefore not caused by a rare-specific false-alarm rate.
findings.evidence: Median FPR over codes with more than 20 training reports (pooled uniform) x 46 rare codes x 661,160 reports: zs_qwen 5.0e-4 -> 15,209; zs_gemma 5.0e-4 -> 15,231; zs_opus 5.0e-4 -> 15,235; rag 2.5-3.75e-4 -> 7,600-11,400; enc 2.5e-4 -> 7,614. Codes with more than 100 training reports: 11,400-22,840. Using the observed mean rare FPR instead gives zs 13,719 / 11,736 / 6,198 (sampled false 166 / 142 / 75 pooled). The year-weighted actual is 14,693 / 14,476 / 6,665. Medians have a resolution of 1.25e-4, so these figures are coarse.

findings.claim: False rare answers concentrate on a few codes: the top 5 codes carry 69-85% of them, and the top 3 carry 49-75%. They do not concentrate on text templates: the false-rare reports cluster no more than a random set of uniform reports of the same size.
findings.evidence: Pooled zero-shot top 1 / 3 / 5 / 10 share: qwen 0.26 / 0.54 / 0.69 / 0.86 (166 sampled false, 25 codes); gemma 0.45 / 0.69 / 0.79 / 0.92 (142, 19 codes); opus 0.29 / 0.64 / 0.75 / 0.88 (75, 17 codes). The 2026 top-5 share alone is 0.69 / 0.85 / 0.83. Templates were built on the union of zero-shot false-rare reports (250) with TF-IDF unigram cosine: at >=0.8 there are 238 templates, 113 needed for 50% and 188 for 80%. A random same-size uniform set gives 240 / 115 / 190. At >=0.6 the false-rare set gives 187 templates (62 for 50%, 137 for 80%) against 210 (85, 160) for the random set, which is only mildly clumpier. Per coder at bigram cos>=0.8 the largest template holds at most 2 reports.

findings.claim: Over-naming is driven by the text, not by the model. The three LLMs give a rare code on the same reports far more often than chance would predict, and nearly always the same code.
findings.evidence: 2026 zero-shot on the uniform draw: sets of 89 (qwen), 88 (gemma) and 41 (opus) reports. Intersections: qwen-gemma 43 (1.96 expected if independent), Jaccard 0.32, same code on 40; qwen-opus 24 (0.91 expected), Jaccard 0.23, same code 21; gemma-opus 32 (0.90 expected), Jaccard 0.33, same code 31. 20 reports appear in all three, 18 of them with the same code. 2025: Jaccard 0.27-0.32, every intersecting report has the same code, 18 in all three. Six rare codes are named falsely by all three LLMs in 2026.

findings.claim: Attractor codes persist from 2025 to 2026 for zero-shot, with no new zero-shot attractors in 2026. Retrieval's false rare codes are less stable.
findings.evidence: Spearman of per-code sampled false counts, 2025 vs 2026, over the 46 rare codes: zs_qwen 0.66, zs_gemma 0.78, zs_opus 0.52; rag 0.18-0.47. Over all known codes: zs 0.79-0.84, rag 0.67-0.73, enc 0.66. Top-5 rare false codes overlap 4 of 5 between years for every zero-shot LLM, 2 of 5 for retrieval. No rare code has 0 zero-shot false answers in 2025 and >=3 in 2026; the only such new case is Battery Problem: High Impedance under rag_qwen (0 to 4).

findings.claim: False rare answers are more literal and less related to the filed code in the tree than false frequent answers. The LLM matches words of a code name in the report rather than the coding convention behind the filed code.
findings.evidence: Pooled uniform, tree relation of false answers (rare / non-rare): zs_qwen unrelated branch 0.70 / 0.49, ancestor-descendant 0.16 / 0.27; zs_gemma 0.75 / 0.49; zs_opus 0.65 / 0.50, sibling 0.19 / 0.14. Encoder non-rare false: unrelated 0.46. Share of reports where the answered term shares a content word with the text versus the filed term: zs_qwen false-rare 0.41 vs 0.26, false-nonrare 0.35 vs 0.25; zs_gemma 0.40 vs 0.33 and 0.37 vs 0.22; zs_opus 0.66 vs 0.30 and 0.39 vs 0.20; right answers 0.65-0.71. The word-match test is a crude prefix test with my own stopword list.

findings.claim: Top attractors and the codes their reports were actually filed as (pooled uniform, zero-shot, any of the 3 LLMs). (1) 'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action' is the only code in the 'No Apparent Adverse Event' branch and has 3 training reports. It is answered falsely on 85 reports (qwen 43, gemma 64, opus 13), all in an unrelated branch: filed Patient Device Interaction Problem 19, Degraded 8, Defective Device 5. It looks like a catch-all for 'device not at fault'. (2) 'Failure to Reset' (25 reports; opus 22, gemma 21): filed as Pumping Stopped on 21, unrelated branch, with texts that literally say 'would not reset' or 'unable to be cleared'. (3) 'Battery Problem: High Impedance' (14 reports): filed as Premature Discharge of Battery on 13, a sibling; a pacemaker template says 'potential high impedance within the battery', and rag_opus repeats it 13 times. (4) 'Application Program Problem: Medication Error' (30, mostly qwen): filed as Computer Software Problem 8 (ancestor) and Labelling/IFU 7; these are Pyxis medstation dispensing texts. (5) 'Pacing Inadequately' (25, mostly qwen): filed as Pacing Problem 8 (parent) and Therapeutic Output Failure 5; it is also used on insulin-pump motor alarms. (6) 'Decoupling' (14): filed as Detachment of Device or Device Component on 10, e.g. tubing that 'came apart'.
findings.evidence: Three snippets of at most 40 words per attractor are stored in results_part2.json 'attractors'. Examples: 'would not reset despite recycling power and battery change' (filed Failure to Infuse); 'data analysis identified potential high impedance within the battery' (filed Premature Discharge of Battery); 'five needles were supposed to be inside, there were six' (Extra Components; filed Manufacturing, Packaging or Shipping Problem). The 'catch-all' reading of Prophylactic removal is my interpretation: keyword shares (no injury 0.25-0.54, recall 0.05-0.62) do not cleanly confirm it.
findings.reproduce: s3_concentration.py section 7b; s4_extra.py 'No Apparent Adverse Event' section

findings.claim: Retrieval removes most zero-shot rare answers on ordinary reports and usually swaps in the filed code. It keeps no false-rare-free gain: on the rare census it also drops about half of the zero-shot answers that were right.
findings.evidence: 2026 uniform draw, reports where zs names a rare code: qwen 89 (rag keeps 11, 0 of them right; drops 77 to a non-rare code, 44 of which match the filed code); gemma 88 (keeps 12, 1 right; drops 75, 51 right); opus 41 (keeps 16, 1 right; drops 25, 18 right). 2025: rag keeps 8 of 77, 9 of 55, 10 of 35. Rare census rows of the natural sample, 2026: rag keeps 38 of 76 (qwen), 51 of 100 (gemma), 46 of 92 (opus) right zs rare answers, and rescues only 3-8 where zs was wrong. In 2025 it keeps 58 of 146, 59 of 108, 53 of 109.

leads: Add a frequency prior to the zero-shot LLM, either as a fixed log-prior added to its code choice or as a two-stage 'is this one of the 46 rare codes at all' gate. Without log-probabilities the practical form is a prior-weighted re-ranking over the zs/rag/enc candidates, fitted on 2024val/2025nat and applied unchanged to 2026. CPU only.

Treat the attractors as a coding-convention problem rather than a model problem. For example, give 'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action' and the other catch-all codes a short definition, or a 'not a device problem' code in the prompt. Test on 2025nat first. Needs a local GPU (Qwen/Gemma) with the user's go-ahead, or API credit.

Reframe the target from labelling rare codes at natural proportions to ranking a review queue: report recall of the 552 rare reports at a fixed review budget, e.g. 0.1% or 0.5% of reports. The flat ~4e-4 per-code FPR makes precision above about 2% impossible for any listed coder (70-150x gap). CPU only, using existing outputs.

Check the attractor list against 2024val (training-year natural sample) to see whether a per-code false-name screen chosen on 2024/2025 removes the top 5 attractors in 2026. Persistence (Spearman 0.52-0.78, 4 of 5 top codes repeat) suggests it should. CPU only.

Have a human (the user or a domain expert) read the top-attractor reports and judge whether the LLM's code is defensible. If many are, the 'false' rare answers partly measure label noise or filing conventions, not model error.
caveats: The uniform draws hold 4,000 reports a year, and only 4 of the 8,000 pooled reports carry a rare filed code. Per-code FPR for rare codes therefore rests on 0-64 sampled false answers per code, medians are mostly 0, and FPR resolution is 1.25e-4 (pooled). The band-mean FPR is the stable statistic; medians are coarse.
Pooling 2025 and 2026 for FPR and slope uses 2026 answers. That is descriptive, not a test. Nothing here was tuned or chosen with 2026 answers.

The template clustering (TF-IDF cosine, connected components) follows the brief's definition. It does not group the pacemaker 'code 1003' battery reports at bigram cos>=0.8: they share a phrase but differ elsewhere. So the claim 'templates do not explain over-naming' holds for whole-text similarity, not for shared key phrases.
The manufacturer field came back empty for these pool rows, so the manufacturer breakdown is uninformative.
The lexical-overlap test is crude: word prefix match with my own stopword list. Treat it as directional only.
Implied precision uses the band-average per-code prevalence and band TPR from 2026 year-weighted rows. It is an approximation, not a per-code estimate.
Year counts follow the repo's convention of adding the balanced 2026 rows (weight 1) to the natural sample.
surprises: Per code, rare codes are named falsely no more often than frequent codes. The zero-shot mean FPR on the 1-5 band (2.0-4.5e-4) is about the median for codes with more than 20 training reports (5.0e-4), and the counterfactual leaves false rare answers unchanged or higher.
Zero-shot answer frequency is essentially independent of training frequency below 100 training reports (Poisson slope -0.07 to 0.11), so the LLM behaves like a near-uniform prior over the tail.
False-rare reports are not more templated than random reports at cos>=0.8 (113 vs 115 templates for 50%), even though one famous template (pacemaker 'high impedance within the battery') exists.
'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action' is the only code under 'No Apparent Adverse Event'. It alone draws 26-45% of zero-shot false rare answers for Qwen and Gemma, and 85 reports in total.
Retrieval brings the frequency prior back (slope 0.89-0.93), and that is exactly why it drops about half of the right zero-shot rare answers on the rare census.

checks.claim: The loader reproduces encoder 2026 32 right / 166 false a year (uniform accuracy 0.6365), 2025 60 / 1 (0.7482), and the zero-shot and retrieval 2026 year counts
checks.detail: Measured with my own loader. It reads the stored outputs through ms.load_coders with the text scan skipped, and computes the weights myself from the natural-split JSON. Encoder 2026: 32.0 / 166.0, with 1 sampled false. Zero-shot (zs) 2026: Qwen 131 / 14,693.4 (88 sampled false), Gemma 158 / 14,476.0 (87), Opus 154 / 6,664.7 (40). Retrieval (rag) 2026: 79 / 2,733.5 (16), 92 / 2,235.2 (13), 95 / 3,025.6 (18). Uniform accuracy is 0.6365 for 2026 and 0.7482 for 2025. Weights check out. The balanced set shares 0 report keys with the natural sample in both years, so nothing is counted twice. The natural weights sum to the candidate pool (657,204 in 2026). Adding the 3,956 balanced rows gives exactly 661,160 known-code reports. The uniform weight is 164.025 (2026) and 189.512 (2025). The rare definition (1-5 training reports) gives 46 codes. There are 6 codes at exactly 6 reports and 47 codes with 0, so an off-by-one would show, and there is none.

checks.claim: Over-naming ratios by band on the pooled uniform draw (N=8,000): zs 1-5 band 41.5 / 35.8 / 19.0; rag 6.5-7.5; enc 0.25. Sampled 1-5 band answers: zs 166 / 143 / 76
checks.detail: Measured: filed share 0.0005 / 0.0046 / 0.011 / 0.116 / 0.868 (4 / 37 / 88 / 928 / 6,943 reports). Ratios for the bands 1-5 / 6-20 / 21-100 / 101-1000 / >1000: zs_qwen 41.5 / 3.0 / 2.64 / 2.46 / 0.75; zs_gemma 35.75 / 6.65 / 1.88 / 2.46 / 0.74; zs_opus 19.0 / 6.95 / 2.23 / 1.63 / 0.85; rag 6.5 / 6.75 / 7.5 on the 1-5 band; enc 0.25 / 1.03 / 0.68 / 0.90 / 1.02. All match the report. The denominator of the 1-5 band rests on only 4 pooled reports (2 per year), so the ratio's scale is coarse. The ordering is not in doubt.

checks.claim: Mean per-code FPR per band, rare (1-5) band zs 4.51 / 3.86 / 2.04 e-4, flat up to 21-100; Spearman(FPR, training count) zs 0.41-0.65, enc and rag 0.76-0.78
checks.detail: Measured, same numbers. Means x1e-4 for the bands 1-5 / 6-20 / 21-100 / 101-1000 / >1000: zs_qwen 4.51 / 3.48 / 4.56 / 15.62 / 32.24; zs_gemma 3.86 / 7.94 / 3.20 / 15.49 / 28.87; zs_opus 2.04 / 8.11 / 3.77 / 9.54 / 30.73. rag on the 1-5 band is 0.71-0.79 and enc is 0.03. Spearman: enc 0.78, rag 0.76-0.78, zs 0.41 / 0.50 / 0.65. Caveat (inferred): the rare-band mean is set by a few attractor codes, since the top 5 codes carry 69-79% of the false answers and most rare codes have 0 false answers. By the median, rare codes are named falsely less often than frequent ones (0 against 5e-4). 'As often as' holds for the mean only.

checks.claim: Counterfactual: the median FPR of codes with more than 20 training reports x 46 x 661,160 gives about 15,200 (zs), 7,600-11,400 (rag and enc). The observed mean rare FPR gives 13,719 / 11,736 / 6,198
checks.detail: Measured: zs 15,209 / 15,231 / 15,235; rag 11,409 / 11,405 / 7,611; enc 7,614. With the observed mean rare FPR: 13,719 / 11,736 / 6,198. The arithmetic is right. The conclusion drawn from it is weaker than worded. The comparison sets a frequent-code median against a rare-code mean that attractors dominate. It shows that the per-code false rate on rare codes is not unusual. It does not show that there is no bias: the 19-41x over-naming against prevalence, and the flat Poisson slope, are that bias, namely the missing frequency prior. The headline does in fact say this.

checks.claim: Poisson slope of answer count on log training share, all known codes / codes with <=100 training reports: gold 0.88 / 0.65, enc 0.94 / 0.61, zs 0.48 / 0.09, 0.49 / -0.07, 0.64 / 0.11, rag 0.90 / 0.35, 0.89 / 0.18, 0.93 / 0.12
checks.detail: Measured with an unpenalised sklearn PoissonRegressor on the pooled uniform draw, over the 424 codes with at least 1 training report. Every value matches to 2 decimals.

checks.claim: Concentration: zs false rare answers have a top-1/3/5 code share of 0.26/0.54/0.69 (Qwen, 166 false over 25 codes), 0.45/0.69/0.79 (Gemma, 142 over 19), 0.29/0.64/0.75 (Opus, 75 over 17)
checks.detail: Measured, identical numbers. I did not recompute the 2026-only top-5 shares, the year-to-year Spearman persistence, the template clustering or the lexical-overlap test.

checks.claim: The three LLMs name a rare code on the same 2026 uniform reports: intersections 43 / 24 / 32 against 1.96 / 0.91 / 0.90 expected, Jaccard 0.32 / 0.23 / 0.33, same code 40 / 21 / 31; 20 reports in all three, 18 with the same code
checks.detail: Measured, every number reproduced (sets of 89 / 88 / 41 over all 4,000 uniform rows). Calling it text-driven (not model-driven) is an inference, but a reasonable one given an overlap of about 22-35x the overlap expected by chance.

checks.claim: Retrieval removes most zs rare answers on ordinary reports, and on the rare census it keeps only about half of the zs rare answers that were right
checks.detail: Measured, 2026 uniform draw: rag keeps 11 / 12 / 16 of the 89 / 88 / 41 zs rare answers (0 / 1 / 1 of those right). It moves 77 / 75 / 25 to a non-rare code, and 44 / 51 / 18 of those match the filed code. 2026 census: rag keeps 38 of 76, 51 of 100 and 46 of 92 right zs rare answers, and rescues 8 / 3 / 5. 2025: rag keeps 8 of 77, 9 of 55 and 10 of 35 on the uniform draw, and 58 of 146, 59 of 108 and 53 of 109 on the census. All match.

checks.claim: Implied precision about 1% for zs on the 1-5 band. A 50% precision needs FPR of about 3e-6, which is 70-150x below the rare FPR of zs and below the per-code FPR of every coder in every band
checks.detail: Measured: the per-code prevalence of 9.6e-6 is 291/46/661,160, i.e. the natural census only. It leaves out the 261 balanced-test rare reports, which belong to the same 2026 year: the candidate pool excludes them, and 657,204 + 3,956 = 661,160. The true year prevalence is 552/46/661,160 = 1.81e-5, 1.9x higher. Their TPR of 0.26 / 0.34 / 0.32 is also census-only (76 / 100 / 92 of 291). Over all 552 rare reports it is 0.237 / 0.286 / 0.279. Corrected (inferred, arithmetic): the FPR needed for 50% precision is 4.3e-6 / 5.2e-6 / 5.0e-6. The gap to the zs band-mean FPR is about 105x / 74x / 40x, not 70-150x. Precision computed directly from the year counts is 0.9% / 1.1% / 2.3% (Opus is about 2%, not 1%). The phrase 'below every coder in every band' is false: the encoder's mean FPR on the 1-5 band is 0.03e-4 = 3e-6, which is at or below the target. That figure rests on 1 sampled false answer, so it is coarse.

corrections: The rare prevalence and TPR used for the precision bound come from the 291-report census only. Including the 261 balanced-test rare reports (same year, disjoint keys), the per-code prevalence is 1.81e-5, not 9.6e-6. The FPR needed for 50% precision is then 4.3e-6 to 5.2e-6, and the gap to the zero-shot rare FPR is about 40-105x, not 70-150x.
Zero-shot precision on rare codes is 0.9% (Qwen), 1.1% (Gemma) and 2.3% (Opus) from the year counts. 'About 1%' understates Opus.

'70-150x below what any coder shows on any band' is wrong for the encoder. Its rare-band mean FPR is 3e-6 (1 sampled false answer, coarse), already at the target. The statement holds for the zero-shot and retrieval coders only.

'Rare codes are named falsely about as often as typical frequent codes' holds for the band mean, which a handful of attractor codes drive. By the median, rare codes are named falsely less often (0 against 5e-4). The counterfactual compares a frequent-code median with a rare-code mean.
check.net: I recomputed seven of the report's measured claims with my own loader and weights, and they match exactly. These are the sanity counts, the band over-naming ratios, the per-band FPR, the counterfactual, the Poisson slopes, the concentration in a few codes, the overlap between the three LLMs, and what retrieval keeps and drops. No double counting between the balanced and natural parts, no off-by-one in the rare definition, and no key misalignment turned up. The one real error is in the precision bound. It counts only the 291 census rare reports and leaves out the 261 balanced rare reports from the same year. Corrected, the gap is about 40-105x, not 70-150x, zero-shot precision is 1-2%, and the encoder already sits near the required FPR. That error does not change the conclusion. The zero-shot coders behave as if they have almost no frequency prior across the tail, and their false answers are text-driven, shared across models and concentrated on a few attractor codes. Even removing the top 5 attractors (69-79% of the pooled false answers) would cut the false rare answers only 3-5x, far short of a 40-100x gap. So labelling rare codes at natural proportions with these coders cannot reach useful precision, and a review queue or an attractor fix is the better target. The wording 'no special bias' is a matter of framing: per code the false rate is ordinary, but the flat prior is itself the bias against prevalence. I did not recheck the template, lexical and year-to-year persistence claims.

investigations.title: Is the filed code predictable from the text? Templates, label consistency and drift

report.headline: Measured: the filed code follows a filing habit that the 2024 encoder already knows, and the LLM's false rare answers mostly come from reading the text literally. Of the 40 sampled false rare answers from Opus zero-shot in the 2026 uniform draw (about 6,572 a year), the encoder gives the filed code on 31. Two report wordings account for 25 of the 40: a pump that 'could not be reset' (Opus answers Failure to Reset, filed Pumping Stopped, 15) and a pacemaker 'Code 1003, voltage too low' (Opus answers Battery Problem: High Impedance, filed Premature Discharge of Battery, 10). A memory of earlier 2026 filings adds almost nothing: it fixes 1 of the 9 cases the encoder misses. It also cannot find rare codes: 16-17 of the 552 rare 2026 reports have an earlier report with the same opening (same first 200 characters) and the same rare code. Identical texts are filed consistently. In the raw 2026 file, copying the code of an earlier identical report covers 64.8% of single-label reports and is right 96.5% of the time. But the pool removes exactly those reports: it keeps one report per narrative and drops every narrative filed under more than one code. That drop takes out 35.2% of 2026 single-label reports, whose majority code is still right 93.9% of the time. From 2025 to 2026 the encoder loses 0.112 uniform accuracy, and the retrieval coders lose 0.080-0.089. Roughly a quarter of the encoder's loss is more reports without a close 2024 neighbour. About three quarters comes from codes changing at the same similarity, mostly far from any training report, with sibling-code swaps such as Incorrect Readings to Low or High Readings. Zero-shot accuracy did not fall (Opus 0.418 to 0.411), so the text did not get harder to read. What moved was the filing habit relative to 2024.

findings.claim: Loader sanity check passes: encoder 2026 = 32 right / 166 false rare a year (1 sampled false), uniform accuracy 0.6365; 2025 = 60 / 1, accuracy 0.7482.
findings.evidence: rare_limits.load_year + score, all three LLM loads give identical encoder numbers

findings.claim: How the pools are built (5 lines). (1) Text = the first type-D (description of event) narrative of each report only; manufacturer narratives (H10 etc.) are not used. (2) Label = device-problem codes minus non-informative markers (IMDRF A24-A27, 2203 Other, 2204 Unknown, 1, '-'); a report is kept only if exactly one code remains, not 'the first code'. (3) Deduplication: lowercase, normalise whitespace, mask digit runs; one item per narrative (the representative is the smallest report key; n_reports = group size); a narrative filed under more than one code is dropped; for 2025/2026 a narrative already in the 2024 pool is also dropped (one already in the 2025 pool is not). (4) Manufacturer, product_code and generic_name are filled only in 2024 (99.6% / 100% / 99.99%); they are 0.0% filled in 2025 and 2026 because only device2024.zip was used. (5) 2026 = FDA's current-year text file (to 2026-11-04) with problem codes as of 2026-11-04; DATE_REPORT is empty for every row.
findings.evidence: scripts/maude_pool.py, scripts/maude_profile.py, notes/maude-profile-2026-10-06.md; fill rates and key order from s1 (2024 pool 728,395 items standing for 1,372,728 reports; 2025 pool 821,295 / 1,059,165; 2026 pool 712,313 / 1,099,828). findings.claim: Answer to the closing question. Of the 'LLM is wrong on a rare code' count at natural proportions, roughly three quarters (Opus zs 31 of 40 sampled; Qwen and Gemma about 63%) are reports where the filed code is the manufacturer's habitual frequent code. The LLM reads the text literally ('could not be reset', 'high impedance') and picks the matching rare term. That habit is learnable from 2024 filings: the frozen encoder knows it. Online memory of earlier 2026 filings is needed for only about 1 of the 40, and in this deduplicated pool exact-template memory covers 13% of reports at most. The part that only online memory can know is small here. It would be large on raw reports (65% coverage at 96.5%), but the pool removed those reports by design.
findings.evidence: combination of the measured numbers above

leads: CPU: score on raw reports instead of deduplicated narratives, with an exact-template memory first and the coders only for texts not seen before. The raw stream gives 64.8% coverage at 96.5%; check what remains for the LLMs and how many false rare answers survive.

CPU: a frozen 'family veto'. When the encoder (or a 2024 neighbour vote) names a frequent code at moderate cosine, drop an LLM rare answer. 31 of 40 zs-Opus false rare would be vetoed; check how many of the 150-176 reachable rare rights die with them, choosing the threshold on 2025nat only.

CPU: report results at IMDRF level 2 and level 1 as well as the exact code, so that sibling-code drift (Incorrect Readings to Low/High Readings, Charging Problem to Failure to Charge, Leak/Splash to Fluid/Blood Leak) is separated from content errors.

CPU: give the LLM the convention instead of the bare label list: a short 'these phrases are filed as' map built from 2024 (for example, non-resettable malfunction alarm is filed as Pumping Stopped; Code 1003 low voltage is filed as Premature Discharge of Battery). Test on 2025nat, then apply unchanged to 2026. Running the LLMs needs a GPU (with the user's go-ahead) or API credit.

Human / data: manufacturer and product code are empty for 2025/2026 (no device2025/2026 file). Downloading them needs the user's OK. Per-manufacturer filing habits are probably the strongest signal of the filed code.

Reframe (human decision): the better-posed task may be (a) flag reports where the literal reading disagrees with the manufacturer's habitual code, as a consistency or review queue, or (b) detect drift in each manufacturer's filing habit over time, rather than predicting rare codes at natural proportions.
caveats: Time order: foitext2026 has an empty DATE_REPORT, so 'report key follows time' rests on an in-text date proxy from only 149 dated texts. cache_dates2026.pkl holds no usable dates. Beyond this, the raw zip was scanned once for consistency counts, which the task did not ask for.

Sections 2-4 use all 4,000 uniform-stratum rows (including 26 rows that also belong to the rare strata), unweighted. Section 5 and the false-rare counts use the 3,974 frequent-code uniform rows. Yearly figures are the sampled count x 164.3 and are coarse.

The template memory runs on deduplicated pool items, so full-text matches inside 2026 are impossible by construction. The first-200-character hash is a crude proxy for near-duplicates, and 85-128 covered rows match more than one code.

The 2024+2025 memory uses all 2024 pool items (including the 2024 test and validation reports) and all of 2025. These are filed before 2026, so it is legitimate prior knowledge, but it is more than the encoder was trained on.
The decomposition with 6 finer bins was computed by hand from the measured bin shares and accuracies; the 5-bin decomposition was computed in code.
'Answer-term word appears in the text' is a crude proxy for literal reading (word stem of the first 6 letters, first 400 characters only).

Some conflict-narrative and 2024-overlap counts for 2026 are not separated: the claim that about 256k reports were dropped as already in the 2024 pool is arithmetic, not measured, and is left out of the findings.
Nothing was tuned on 2026; all memory rules are fixed (majority code, frequent = more than 20 training reports). The online memory uses 2026 filed codes and is therefore not the frozen protocol.
surprises: Zero-shot accuracy did not fall from 2025 to 2026 (Opus 0.418 to 0.411, Qwen 0.296 to 0.315), while the encoder and retrieval coders lost 0.08-0.11. The drift is in the filing habit relative to 2024, not in how hard the text is to read.

The pool drops every narrative filed under more than one code: 35.2% of 2026 single-label reports. Those narratives still carry their majority code 93.9% of the time, so the evaluation removes the largest and most predictable block of reports.

In 2026 only 0.85% of uniform reports have a 2024 neighbour at cosine 0.98 or above, against 12.7% in 2024val. 91% sit below 0.80, and nearest-neighbour code agreement there fell from 0.535 (2025) to 0.449.
Retrieval Opus still answers Battery Problem: High Impedance on 10 pacemaker 'Code 1003' reports even with 10 labelled 2024 neighbours in the prompt.
Even at IMDRF level 1 (27 top-level codes) Opus zero-shot reaches only 0.688 against the encoder's 0.816. The convention gap is not just a choice between sibling codes.

Qwen 2026: 106 / 14,678 against 25 / 15.8. Gemma 2026: 135 / 14,463 against 23 / 12.8. Coverage and accuracy are therefore probably carried by a small number of very large boilerplate templates. A '96.5% on 65% of reports' figure says little about what a coder must do on new text. corrections: Yearly count for the 40 Opus zs false rare: 6,561 with the real weights (164.02 per row), not 6,572.

The 2025-to-2026 encoder fall is about one third composition and two thirds within-similarity (10 bins or a continuous fit: -0.038 of -0.112), not a quarter and three quarters. The 5-bin split (-0.014) understates composition because nearly all rows sit in one bin. For nearest-neighbour agreement it is about half and half (-0.056 / -0.054), not -0.026 / -0.083.

'The frozen encoder knows the filed code' does not separate false rare answers from right ones. The encoder names a frequent code on 129 of Opus's 154 right rare answers in 2026 (whole year), so the proposed family veto would remove most of the reachable rights. In 2025 dev it would remove 135 of 175.

The two dominant families are each one manufacturer template family (10 and 15 sampled reports, 7 and 13 distinct openings). Yearly counts built on them (about 2,460 and about 1,640) are clustered estimates, not independent samples.
check.net: These numbers reproduce exactly: the loader, the 40 Opus false rare answers (31 where the encoder gives the filed code; the 15 + 10 template pairs), the accuracy changes from 2025 to 2026 (zero-shot flat, encoder and retrieval down 0.08-0.11) and the parent-level accuracies. I found no wrong weights, no double counting (balanced and natural keys do not overlap) and no off-by-one in the rare definition. Nothing they present as clean was chosen on 2026 answers. Two parts of the reading are overstated. First, the drift split: finer or continuous binning gives about one third composition, not one quarter. Second, and more important, 'the habit is learnable, the frozen encoder knows it' is true only of the false answers. The encoder also names a frequent code on 129 of Opus's 154 right rare answers (2026, whole year), so encoder disagreement cannot tell a literal misreading from a true rare report. What follows from the numbers: most false rare answers are literal readings of a few manufacturer templates whose filed code is a frequent sibling. A frozen 2024 coder does not offer a cheap way to remove them without also removing most of the right rare answers. The raw-stream 'copy earlier identical report' result (65% at 96.5%) was not recomputed, and it is likely driven by a few very large templates.

investigations.title: Why does no coder find about 380 of the 552 rare-code reports?

report.headline: The coders miss most 2026 rare-code reports mainly because of the labels, not because they read the text badly. The loader reproduces the known numbers: encoder 32 right / 166 false a year (1 sampled false), uniform accuracy 0.6365. Of the 552 rare reports, 219 have the filed code in at least one of the 7 answers (encoder plus zero-shot and retrieval for 3 LLMs), so 333 are missed by every coder. The misses sit in a few codes that are one manufacturer's filing habit and that grew from 2-5 training reports to 20-80 in 2026. The 3 largest codes hold 129 of the 333 misses and the top 10 hold 234: Omnipod insulin reports filed as 'Medication Error' (68 of 78 missed), iLet VBUCK voltage faults filed as 'Power Conditioning Problem' under the Environmental branch (34 of 34 missed), and Philips ISCV security notices filed under the parent 'Computer System Security Problem' while the LLMs pick a child code. On missed reports the coders mostly agree with each other on a different code: all 3 zero-shot LLMs name the same wrong code on 104 reports and all 3 retrieval runs on 188. I read 40 missed reports by hand (one reader only). In 23 the text supports the coder's answer as well as or better than the filed code, in 6 the filed code looks wrong, in 7 the text says too little, and in only 4 is the coder clearly wrong. Better candidate lists add little: a perfect chooser over encoder top-5 plus all LLM answers plus the 10 neighbours' codes reaches 243/552, and 297/552 even with encoder top-50. The 2025 nearest neighbours also do not help: TF-IDF over all 821k 2025 reports puts the filed code among the 10 neighbours for 72/552. For 'Medication Error', 156 labelled 2025 reports exist, yet only 6 of its 78 2026 reports have one among their neighbours. My answer: mostly a label problem (filing habit and choice of tree level), then a text problem, and only a small coder problem.

Encoder top-k holds the filed code, all 552 / the 333 missed: top-1 32/0, top-3 89/17, top-5 115/23, top-10 143/36, top-20 171/50, top-50 219/78. Median rank on missed reports is 195 of 424. The filed code is among the 10 neighbours' codes for 14 of 552 (2 of the missed); the nearest neighbour has it once.

findings.claim: Reading 40 missed reports spread over codes, most look like filing habit or judgement calls rather than coder mistakes.
findings.evidence: (a) text clearly supports the filed code: 4. (b) text supports a coder's answer as well or better: 23. (c) text says too little: 7. (d) filed code looks wrong: 6. Examples: 'four back-to-back micro insulin bolus ... hypoglycemic' filed Medication Error, Opus says Excess Flow (b). 'persistent power subsystem malfunction ... VBUCK over/under voltage' filed Environmental > Power Conditioning, coders say Power Problem (d/b). 'Olympus flushing pump had continued to run water even though the pedal was no longer pressed' filed Flushing Problem, coders say Device Remains Activated (b). 'during a leak was observed from the D-vial' filed Emergency Power Failure (d). 'burn marks on the primary laser fiber ... potential unwanted laser emission' filed Radiation Leak, coders say Output below Specifications (a).
findings.reproduce: missed_sample.txt (made by c2_analyse.py, seed 7); judgements in reading_40_judgements.txt

findings.claim: With lenient scoring (parent, child or sibling of the filed code also counts), many more rare reports are nearly found.
findings.evidence: Strict -> lenient per answer: enc 32->151, zero-shot Qwen 131->289, Gemma 158->239, Opus 154->255; retrieval Qwen 79->216, Gemma 92->193, Opus 95->200. Any of the 7: 219->357. Per LLM run (enc+zs+rag): Qwen 150->338, Gemma 176->295, Opus 172->302. Tree distance also undercounts: Power Conditioning (Environmental branch) vs Power Problem (Electrical branch) counts as other branch.

findings.claim: A perfect chooser over the candidate set reaches only about 44% of the 552.
findings.evidence: Filed code in encoder top-5: 115. In any of the 6 LLM answers: 217. In the 2024 neighbour codes: 14. Encoder top-5 or LLM: 242. Union of all three: 243 (mean candidate set size 9.9). With encoder top-10/20/50 instead of top-5: 256 / 270 / 297.

findings.claim: Adding labelled 2025 reports through plain TF-IDF nearest neighbours barely raises the ceiling, even for codes with many 2025 examples.
findings.evidence: Index: all 821,295 2025 pool reports, word 1-2 grams, k=10. Filed code among the 10 neighbours' codes: 72 of 552; top-1: 20. Per code, top-1 / top-10: Medication Error (156 labelled 2025 reports) 1/78 and 6/78; Implant subsidence 9/63 and 38/63; Decoupling 4/27 and 7/27; Power Conditioning, both Security codes and Flushing Problem 0. As a coder: majority-of-10 gives 13 right / 0 false (0 sampled); top-1 with no cut-off gives 20 right / 169 false (1 sampled). Uniform accuracy of top-1 is 0.5873 on frequent-code rows.

findings.claim: The low ceiling is mainly a label problem, then a text problem; the coder problem is the smallest part.
findings.evidence: Label side: the misses come from a few new manufacturer habits. Coders agree with each other on another code, the reading put 29/40 in (b)+(d), and 2025 examples of the same code do not resemble the 2026 texts. Text side: 7/40 say too little. Coder side: only 4/40 are clear coder errors, and better candidate lists lift the perfect-chooser ceiling only from 243 to 297.

leads: Score at the level of the tree or a nearby group of codes rather than the exact leaf; it fits how filers choose codes. Lenient recall per LLM run is 295-338 of 552 against 150-176 strict. The false side under lenient scoring on the uniform draw still has to be measured; it is not measured here. CPU only.

Reframe the task as finding new filing habits: flag codes whose yearly volume jumps (Power Conditioning 5 -> 34, Security Problem 14 -> 67, Medication Error 4 -> 156 -> 78), or (manufacturer/device, code) clusters, instead of putting a rare code on single reports. The pools have no manufacturer or product_code values, so this needs the device file (device2024.zip, which is in data/maude). CPU only.

Measure label noise directly: for frequent codes, how often near-duplicate texts carry different filed codes, both within one year and between 2024 and 2025. This gives an estimate of the ceiling any coder could reach. CPU only.

Give a human 'top-k plus tree context' as a review aid instead of a single answer. Encoder top-20 plus LLM answers holds the filed code for 270 of 552 (about 49%); the size and cost of such a review list on frequent reports still needs measuring. CPU only.
Have a second reader repeat the 40-report reading (missed_sample.txt) to check the a/b/c/d split, which comes from one reader. Human.

Retrain the encoder with 2025 reports added; 2025 is fair to use before 2026. Expect little gain for the 2026-only habits (Power Conditioning, Security), some for Decoupling and Implant subsidence. Needs the GPU, so the user's go-ahead first.
caveats: The a/b/c/d reading of 40 reports was done by one reader (me), with no second coder; treat the split as a rough guess. The 40 were spread over codes (round-robin, seed 7), so they over-represent small codes compared with the 333 missed.
'Missed' here means none of all 7 answers is right, across all three LLM runs. Per LLM run the missed count is 552 minus 150/176/172.

Tree relations come from the path strings. Codes that mean nearly the same thing but sit in different branches (Power Conditioning vs Power Problem; Fungus in Device Environment vs Microbial Contamination) count as other branch, so lenient scoring undercounts how close the answers are.
Only the rare-report side of lenient scoring was measured. How many false near-rare answers lenient scoring would add on ordinary reports was not computed.

The TF-IDF 2025 neighbour test is one plain retriever with fixed settings (min_df 5, 200k features, 1-2 grams, text cut at 1,500 characters), not a tuned or embedding retriever. The cosine cut-off rows are descriptive; picking one after seeing them would be hindsight. Its yearly false counts rest on 0-1 sampled uniform rows (one row is about 164 reports a year), so they are very coarse.

The pool rows have empty manufacturer, product_code and generic_name fields, so manufacturer clusters are inferred from the text: Omnipod, iLet, Philips ISCV, Olympus and Boston Scientific templates. They are not counted.
2025 per-code counts are from data/maude/pool_codes_2025.json (whole 2025 pool), not from the 2025 samples.
surprises: 'Power Conditioning Problem' has 34 reports in 2026 against 5 in 2025, all from what look like iLet power-rail alert texts. No coder ever names it, and its tree path is in the Environmental branch although the texts describe internal electronics.

'Medication Error' had 156 labelled reports in 2025, yet only 6 of its 78 2026 reports have a 2025 Medication Error report among their 10 TF-IDF neighbours. The same kind of insulin-pump text seems to be filed under several codes.

For 'Computer System Security Problem' the LLMs are close but at the wrong level: they choose the child code 'Application Security Problem' (39 of 67 zero-shot Opus answers), while the manufacturer files the parent. Meanwhile 'Application Security Problem' reports themselves are often missed.

For two pacemaker/ICD templates ('Voltage too low for projected remaining capacity'), the same text is filed as 'Battery Problem: High Impedance' in one report and 'Loss of Threshold' in another, while all coders and all 10 neighbours say 'Premature Discharge of Battery'.

The 2024 neighbours hold the filed code for only 14 of 552 rare reports, so the retrieval coder can rarely copy a rare code from its examples. Its 79-95 right rare answers must come from the code list in the prompt rather than from the examples (inferred).

checks.claim: The loader reproduces the baseline: encoder 2026 has 32 right and 166 false rare answers a year (1 sampled false), uniform accuracy is 0.6365, there are 552 rare reports (261 balanced + 291 census), and some coder is right on 150 / 176 / 172 reports in the Qwen / Gemma / Opus runs.
checks.detail: Measured with my own loader (k1.py, k2.py). load_coders was called with the text read replaced by a stub, since only text_len uses the text. Encoder: 32.0 right, 166.0 false, 1 sampled false. Accuracy on all 4,000 U rows is 0.6365 (0.6397 on the 3,974 rows at weight 164.025). 552 rare reports = 261 + 291. Per-run any-right is 150 / 176 / 172. Checks on the counting: no report key appears in both the balanced and natural sets, and there are no duplicate keys. No rare-code report falls in the uniform draw. All 291 census rows have weight 1. The rare definition c in 1..5 gives 46 codes; the 6 codes with c = 6 are correctly left out. Keys, gold codes and encoder answers are identical across the three LLM loads. The pool_codes_2026 count equals the sample count for every one of the 43 rare codes present, so the census is complete.

checks.claim: 333 of the 552 are missed by all 7 answers and 219 are found by at least one. Per-answer recall: enc 32, zero-shot 131/158/154, retrieval 79/92/95.
checks.detail: Measured: every number matches (219 found, 333 missed).

checks.claim: The misses sit in a few codes: 129 in the top 3 codes, 173 in the top 5, 234 in the top 10 ('in order of code size'). Per-code missed/total, and growth from training count to 2025 pool to 2026 (e.g. Medication Error 2 -> 156 -> 78).
checks.detail: Measured. The per-code figures all match: Medication Error 68/78, Power Conditioning 34/34, Security 27/67, Decoupling 25/27, Prophylactic removal 19/27, Application Security 16/21, Flushing 16/17, RFI 12/18, Implant subsidence 4 missed of 63. The growth counts match: 2->156->78, 4->14->67, 4->109->63, 3->5->34, 5->38->27, 3->24->27, 2->2->21. The top-3 / top-5 codes by size hold 208 / 270 reports. Five codes with 21 or more 2025 pool reports hold 205 reports and 120 misses. The concentration figures are mislabelled: 129/173/234 is what you get when codes are sorted by their number of misses. Sorted by code size, as the finding and headline say, the top 3 / 5 / 10 codes hold 99 / 134 / 215 misses. The lead also gives Medication Error as '4 -> 156 -> 78', but its training count is 2.

checks.claim: On missed reports the coders agree on another code: all 3 zero-shot LLMs give the same wrong code on 104 of 333 (encoder too on 40), at least 2 agree on 238, all 3 retrieval runs agree on 188 (encoder too on 76), and all 7 answers are identical on 25.
checks.detail: Measured: 104 / 40 / 238 / 188 / 76 / 25 all match.

checks.claim: Encoder top-k recall on all 552 / the 333 missed is 32/0, 89/17, 115/23, 143/36, 171/50 and 219/78 for k = 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50. Median rank on missed reports is 195. The 2024 neighbours hold the filed code for 14 reports (2 missed). A perfect chooser over encoder top-5 + LLM answers + neighbour codes reaches 243; with top-10/20/50 it reaches 256/270/297.
checks.detail: Measured: everything matches except top-50 on all 552, where I get 218 against their 219 (probably tie or ordering handling; it does not matter). The encoder has 424 classes and all 46 rare codes are among them. As a check on my ranking, the argmax of the stored probabilities equals the stored encoder answer on 99.2% / 99.3% of rare rows.

checks.claim: Lenient scoring (parent, child or sibling also counts) lifts the any-of-7 count from 219 to 357; per answer, enc 151, zs 289/239/255, rag 216/193/200.
checks.detail: Measured with my own path-string relation: every number matches. They left the false side unmeasured, so I measured it on the uniform draw. Of the zero-shot rare answers that are false on the uniform rows, lenient scoring would count 15 of 88 (Qwen), 16 of 87 (Gemma) and 12 of 40 (Opus) as near-right. For retrieval it is 7 of 16, 3 of 13 and 12 of 18. So under lenient scoring most zero-shot false rare answers stay false: 73, 71 and 28 sampled rows, each standing for about 164 reports a year.

checks.claim: Plain TF-IDF neighbours over all 821k 2025 reports put the filed code among the 10 neighbours for 72 of 552, and for Medication Error only 6/78 despite 156 labelled 2025 reports.
checks.detail: Not recomputed: it needs a full scan of the 2025 pool and a TF-IDF index, which I skipped to keep the machine light. I did confirm the 156 (pool_codes_2025.json). Their yearly false counts for the kNN coder (169 false) rest on 1 sampled uniform row, so they are coarse, as they say.

checks.claim: Conclusion: the low ceiling is mainly a label problem (filing habit, tree level), then a text problem, and only a small coder problem.
checks.detail: Inferred. The measured facts hold: misses concentrate in a few codes that grew sharply, the filed code ranks low, the coders agree on another code, and better candidate lists help little. But those facts do not by themselves separate 'label' from 'coder'. The three LLMs share one prompt and one code list, so their agreement is not independent evidence that the text supports their answer. And a manufacturer convention that is consistent within 2026 (e.g. iLet VBUCK -> Power Conditioning, 34/34) is something a coder could learn, so it is a learnable regularity rather than noise. The split into 4 coder errors / 23 judgement calls / 6 wrong labels / 7 too-little-text comes from one reader on 40 reports drawn round-robin over codes, which does not represent the 333. 'Label problem' is a reasonable reading. 'Only a small coder problem' is not shown.

corrections: Miss concentration 'in order of code size' is 99 / 134 / 215 for the top 3 / 5 / 10 codes. The quoted 129 / 173 / 234 is the figure when codes are sorted by their own miss count. The headline's '3 largest codes hold 129 of the 333 misses' should say 'the 3 codes with the most misses'.
Medication Error has 2 training reports, not 4 (the lead says '4 -> 156 -> 78').
Encoder top-50 holds the filed code for 218 of 552 in my run (theirs 219); the 78 on missed reports matches.

Lenient scoring does not fix the false side: on the uniform draw only 15/88 (Qwen), 16/87 (Gemma), 12/40 (Opus) zero-shot false rare answers become near-right, so most of the roughly 14,000 / 6,700 false a year remain.

The conclusion that the coder problem is small is a guess, not a measured result. LLM agreement on a shared prompt is not independent support, and the 40-report reading comes from one reader on a sample that does not represent the 333.
check.net: Nearly all of the measured numbers survive my own recount. The baseline is 32/166 (1 sampled false) with accuracy 0.6365. The coders find 219 and miss 333 of the 552. Per-code misses, coder agreement on missed reports (104/188/25), encoder top-k recall, the perfect-chooser ceilings 243 to 297, and lenient recall 357 all reproduce. I found no double counting, weight error, off-by-one in the rare definition or key misalignment. There are two errors. The concentration figures labelled 'by code size' (129/173/234) are really sorted by miss count; by size they are 99/134/215. And Medication Error's training count in the lead should be 2, not 4. Lenient scoring would turn only about 15-30% of the zero-shot false rare answers on ordinary reports into near-hits, so it does not remove the false-answer problem. The 'mostly a label problem, small coder problem' conclusion is plausible but rests on one reader's 40-report guess and on LLM agreement that is not independent evidence. The 2025 TF-IDF claim was not rechecked.

investigations.title: Signals not yet used to accept or reject an LLM rare answer

report.headline: There is information the selector does not use, and nearly all of it comes from one signal: the encoder's own probability (or rank) for the rare code the LLM proposed. Over each LLM's rare proposals in 2026 it separates right from false with a weighted AUC of 0.82 to 0.90. The other signals do worse: TF-IDF closeness to the code's own training reports 0.74-0.85, agreement between LLMs 0.56-0.77, word overlap with the code's term 0.33-0.64 (it flips direction for Opus in 2026), and the code appearing among the 10 neighbours 0.53-0.54. A logistic model on all 13 features, fitted on 2025, is no better than encoder log-probability alone. Picking points with 2026 answers (hindsight, like the known best points), encoder log-probability gets about 15-30 more right rare answers a year at the same 1-2 sampled false reports: Gemma 74/166 (1) against 56/198 (1); Qwen 70/167 (1) against 42/214 (1); Opus 75/330 (2) against 58/380 (2). With thresholds frozen on 2025, the gain mostly shrinks: a cut with 0 sampled false in 2025 gives 4-6 sampled false in 2026 (Opus 97/998.5 (6), Gemma 95/669.5 (4), Qwen 91/998.5 (6), encoder base). So the encoder's score for the proposed code shifts the frontier a little, but only in hindsight, and inside the sampling noise, since one sampled report stands for about 164 a year. The other signals mostly land on the same trade-off or are too small to matter. When LLMs agree with each other, the error is shared, not cancelled.

findings.claim: The loader reproduces the known encoder numbers.
findings.evidence: 2026 encoder: 32 right / 166 false rare a year (1 sampled), uniform accuracy 0.6365. 2025: 60 / 1 (0), 0.7482. Rare-proposal right counts match the known zero-shot and retrieval figures (2026 zs right 131 / 158 / 154; rag right 79 / 92 / 95). 2024 training rare-code reports: 132 across 46 codes, no count mismatches.
findings.reproduce: s1_cache.py, s2_train_texts.py, s3_features.py (logs next to them)

findings.claim: (a) The encoder's log-probability for the proposed code is the strongest signal by far.
findings.evidence: Weighted AUC over the LLM's rare proposals (zs and rag pooled), 2025 / 2026: Qwen 0.887 / 0.898, Gemma 0.930 / 0.882, Opus 0.917 / 0.818. Cut at encoder rank <= 10, kept (pass) against dropped (fail), right / false a year (sampled false), 2026: Qwen pass 133 / 1153.2 (7), fail 77 / 16273.7 (97); Gemma pass 132 / 671.9 (4), fail 118 / 16039.3 (96); Opus pass 144 / 826.1 (5), fail 105 / 8864.2 (53). 2025: Qwen 185 / 398.6 (2), Gemma 196 / 592 (3), Opus 191 / 766.9 (4).

findings.claim: (b) When the proposed code is among the 10 neighbours, the proposal is almost never false, but this covers few reports.
(c) TF-IDF closeness to the code's own 1-5 training reports separates moderately. The margin over the nearest neighbour is almost never positive.
findings.evidence: tf_rare AUC 2025 / 2026: Qwen 0.752 / 0.847, Gemma 0.835 / 0.792, Opus 0.781 / 0.737. tf_margin >= 0 passes only 10-12 right with 0-1 false in 2025, and 1 right / 0 false in 2026. The nearest training report of any code was approximated by the nearest of the 10 embedding neighbours, not a full TF-IDF search over all 656,460 training reports.

findings.claim: (d) Word overlap with the code's term is weak and unstable. For Opus in 2026 it points the wrong way.
findings.evidence: Share of the term's content words found in the text (lex) AUC 2025 / 2026: Qwen 0.734 / 0.639, Gemma 0.725 / 0.591, Opus 0.600 / 0.333. Opus 2026 with lex >= 0.5: 156 right / 6640.1 false (40 sampled) kept against 93 / 3050.1 (18) dropped. This fits the template example (a battery text with the word 'impedance' gets the Battery Problem: High Impedance code).

findings.claim: (e) Agreement between LLMs does not clean up the false answers. The LLMs share the same errors.
findings.evidence: Zero-shot rare code named by two or three LLMs, right / false a year (sampled), 2026: Qwen+Gemma 109 / 6655.8 (40), Qwen+Opus 106 / 3501.7 (21), Gemma+Opus 124 / 4958.7 (30), all three 99 / 2977.4 (18). 2025: all three 125 / 3430.5 (18). The xllm signal (number of other LLMs agreeing) has AUC 0.73-0.77 for Qwen and Gemma, but only 0.56-0.57 for Opus.

findings.claim: (f) A high top-1 neighbour cosine (template-like text) goes with false proposals. Low novelty is a warning sign.
findings.evidence: nb_cos AUC 0.32-0.43 in both years, below 0.5, so high cosine means false. With nb_cos >= 0.8 in 2026, the passing proposals are all false: Qwen 0 / 1160.6 (7), Gemma 0 / 502.5 (3), Opus 0 / 1 (0). In 2025 a few right ones pass: Qwen 10 / 2670 (14), Opus 7 / 1139.1 (6).

findings.claim: A combined logistic model on 13 features (fitted on 2025, frozen) is no better than encoder log-probability alone.
findings.evidence: Combined AUC 2025 / 2026: Qwen 0.875 / 0.911, Gemma 0.928 / 0.896, Opus 0.899 / 0.839. Encoder-base systems with thresholds frozen on 2025, results in 2026: combined Opus 85 / 665.5 (4) and 96 / 668.5 (4); Gemma 53 / 330 (2) and 103 / 500.1 (3); Qwen 47 / 330 (2) and 110 / 1679.8 (10). Encoder log-probability alone, frozen threshold -5.863: Opus 97 / 998.5 (6), Gemma 95 / 669.5 (4), Qwen 91 / 998.5 (6). The combined model's coefficients are largest on enc_logp and neg_log_rank.

findings.claim: Thresholds set on 2025 do not carry over to 2026 at the low-false end.
findings.evidence: Encoder log-probability cut with 0 sampled false in 2025 (Opus 130 / 10.9, Gemma 129 / 24.2, Qwen 125 / 19.2) gives 6, 4 and 6 sampled false in 2026 (998.5 / 669.5 / 998.5 a year). 2025 is the easier year (encoder accuracy 0.748 against 0.637).

findings.claim: In hindsight on 2026, encoder log-probability moves the frontier modestly above the known best points.
findings.evidence: Encoder base, threshold picked on 2026: Gemma 74 / 166 (1) and 81 / 334 (2), against the known 56 / 198 (1). Opus 75 / 330 (2) and 94 / 833.5 (5), against the known 58 / 380 (2) and 94 / 873 (5). Prior-corrected base, Qwen: 36 / 3 (0), 70 / 167 (1), 77 / 333 (2), against the known 36 / 63 (0) and 42 / 214 (1). The false side differs by at most 1 sampled report. The right side comes mostly from census rows (weight 1).

findings.claim: A veto on the rule 'encoder base, accept when zs and rag agree on a rare code', using the best single signal chosen on 2025 (encoder rank for Qwen and Gemma, encoder log-probability for Opus), with the threshold set on 2025.
findings.evidence: 2026 without veto: Qwen 80 / 1888 (11), Gemma 99 / 2041.8 (12), Opus 98 / 2681.2 (16). Veto keeping 75% of 2025 right: Qwen 63 / 330 (2), Gemma 69 / 502.5 (3), Opus 75 / 1000.5 (6). Keeping 50%: Qwen 55 / 166 (1), Gemma 54 / 171.4 (1), Opus 52 / 333 (2). Every total includes the encoder's own 32 / 166 (1).

findings.claim: The unused information is essentially a softened agreement between encoder and LLM: the encoder ranks the LLM's rare code high without picking it first. It adds some reach beyond exact agreement but cannot reach the roughly 400 rare reports a year where no coder is right.
findings.evidence: Even at about 17k false a year, the LLM rare proposals that are right number only 210-250 of 552 rare reports in 2026. The best points give about 70-100 right a year.

leads: Treat 'encoder log-probability for the LLM's proposed code' as a selector feature, refit the selector on 2024 and score once on 2026 (CPU only).
Use encoder log-probability in a review queue instead of auto-acceptance: rank the LLM rare proposals by it and report how many right ones fall in the top-k reports a month (CPU only).
Make the 2025-to-2026 threshold transfer more robust, for example by setting the threshold on 2024val plus 2025nat together, or by targeting a false rate instead of a count (CPU only).

Add a template veto: a high top-1 neighbour cosine whose neighbour codes all differ from the proposed rare code. In 2026 nb_cos >= 0.8 catches 7 sampled false for Qwen and 3 for Gemma with 0 right lost (CPU only).
Run a full TF-IDF or BM25 nearest-neighbour search over all 656k training reports to replace the 10-neighbour approximation in signal (c) (CPU only, memory-heavy).

Ask the LLM to rank or justify against the code definition, or ask a verification question ('is this report about X rather than Y'), to test whether a reasoning check breaks the shared literal-reading error. This needs API or GPU and the user's go-ahead.
Increase the uniform draw, or draw extra reports where some LLM proposes a rare code, so that differences of 1-2 sampled false can be told apart (needs LLM outputs on more reports: API or GPU).
caveats: Every comparison with the known best points that uses thresholds picked on 2026 is hindsight. The frozen 2025 thresholds give weaker 2026 points.
Differences on the false side are 0-2 sampled reports, each standing for about 164 a year. They are within sampling noise. AUCs depend on 46-104 sampled false proposals per LLM-year.

Signal (c)'s 'nearest training report of any code' is the TF-IDF max over the 10 embedding neighbours only, not a full search. The TF-IDF vocabulary was fitted on a 27,397-report uniform training sample plus the 132 rare-code reports.
The encoder output covers 424 classes, not all 471 codes. A proposed code missing from the encoder gets log-probability -30 and the last rank. I did not count how many proposals this affects.
Weighted AUC uses whole-year weights, so it is dominated by the uniform-draw false proposals. The per-arm AUCs (zs / rag) are in signals_results.json.
The combined model uses class-balanced sample weights and C=0.3. These were not tuned, and nothing about it was chosen with 2026 answers.
The first feature run was stopped (slow npz access, and pandas is not installed) and rerun after a fix. The final outputs come from the fixed run.
surprises: Word overlap with the code's term points the wrong way for Opus in 2026 (AUC 0.333) after pointing the right way in 2025 (0.600). Template texts that literally contain the term words drive the false answers.
All three LLMs naming the same rare code in 2026 is still mostly false: 99 right against 2977.4 false (18 sampled).
Adding 12 other features to encoder log-probability does not help, and its frozen 2026 points are often worse.

The proposed code appearing among the 10 retrieval neighbours is clean in both years (1 false a year, 0 sampled) but covers only 16-56 right a year. The retrieval LLM evidently proposes rare codes mostly when the neighbours do not contain them.

checks.claim: The loader reproduces encoder 2026 = 32 right / 166 false (1 sampled), uniform accuracy 0.6365; 2025 = 60 / 1 (0), 0.7482.
checks.detail: Measured with my own script c1.py, which uses rare_limits.load_year: the same numbers for all three LLM loads. I also checked the things the task asked me to look for. (1) The balanced and natural parts share no report keys (overlap 0 in 2025 and in 2026), so nothing is counted twice. (2) The rare reports add up: 261 balanced + 291 census = 552 in 2026, and 273 + 324 = 597 in 2025. (3) Whole-year weights are 1, 3.386 and 164.025 in 2026 (1, 1.875 and 189.512 in 2025). The uniform draw has 3,974 rows (2026). (4) The rare definition is c in [1,5], with RARE_MAX = 5, giving 46 codes. (5) The stored enc arm matches the npz argmax on 99.4-100% of rows. (6) None of the 46 rare codes is missing from the encoder's 424 classes, so the investigator's caveat about a -30 fill value affects 0 proposals (measured).

checks.claim: (a) Encoder log-probability of the proposed rare code separates right from false with weighted AUC 0.82-0.90 (2026), and the rank<=10 cut gives the stated pass/fail counts.
checks.detail: My own proposal table and sklearn's weighted roc_auc_score, 2025 / 2026: Qwen 0.887 / 0.898, Gemma 0.930 / 0.882, Opus 0.917 / 0.818. These match exactly. Rank<=10 in 2026, pass: Qwen 133 / 1153.2 (7), Gemma 132 / 671.9 (4), Opus 144 / 826.1 (5). Fail: 77 / 16273.7 (97), 118 / 16039.3 (96), 105 / 8864.2 (53). 2025 pass counts also match. Caveat: the weighted AUC is dominated by the uniform-draw false rows (each weighted 164). Unweighted AUCs are lower: 2026 Qwen 0.882, Gemma 0.843, Opus 0.804. The 2026 AUCs rest on 104, 100 and 58 sampled false proposals.

Measured from neighbors_full.json with my own code matching: exactly these numbers. The '1 false a year' comes from a balanced or census row (weight 1), with 0 sampled. So 'almost never false' rests on 0 sampled uniform rows. With about 3,974 sampled reports, that cannot rule out a few hundred false a year.

checks.claim: (e) All three LLMs agreeing on a zero-shot rare code is still mostly false: 2026 99 / 2977.4 (18), 2025 125 / 3430.5 (18).
checks.detail: Measured, exactly the same numbers. 18 sampled false reports is a solid count, so 'shared error' rests on more than one or two sampled rows. I did not recompute the pairwise combinations.

checks.claim: Thresholds frozen on 2025 do not carry over: the encoder-logp cut with 0 sampled false in 2025 (threshold -5.863) gives 2026 Opus 97 / 998.5 (6), Gemma 95 / 669.5 (4), Qwen 91 / 998.5 (6).
checks.detail: The numbers are confirmed (measured): the same threshold -5.863 for all three LLMs, 2025 at 130 / 10.9, 129 / 24.2 and 125 / 19.2, and 2026 as stated. The threshold is the same because the encoder log-probs are shared across LLMs. The general claim depends on their selection rule, which takes the most right answers with 0 sampled false. That rule is the loosest cut still showing 0 sampled false, so it picks where noise looks best. A more cautious 2025-only rule (at most 5 false a year in 2025; I chose this rule after seeing their results, so it is not blind) gives thresholds -4.18 / -4.18 / -4.40. In 2026 these give Qwen 75 / 494.1 (3), Gemma 76 / 330 (2), Opus 78 / 495.1 (3). That is roughly on or a bit above the known Opus hindsight points (58 / 380 (2), 94 / 873 (5)). So 'the gain shrinks when frozen' holds for their rule, but not for every reasonable 2025 rule. Either way the differences are 1-3 sampled reports.

'Thresholds set on 2025 do not carry over' is specific to their rule (most right answers with 0 sampled false in 2025). That covers the encoder sanity check, the encoder-logp AUCs, the rank<=10 split, the neighbour-hit counts, the three-LLM agreement counts, the frozen -5.863 threshold results and the hindsight points. I found no double counting (balanced and natural parts share no keys), no wrong weights, no off-by-one in the rare definition and no misaligned keys. The conclusion mostly follows from the numbers. The encoder's own score for the LLM's proposed code is the only strong unused signal. Agreement between LLMs does not cancel errors (18 sampled false even when all three agree). The gains over the known best points are about 15-40 right answers a year, and they sit on the weight-1 census side. On the false side the differences are 0-3 sampled reports, too few to tell apart. One correction: 'the gain shrinks when frozen' depends on their loose 2025 rule. A stricter 2025 rule lands near the known frontier in 2026, so the honest summary is 'no clear gain and no clear loss, within sampling noise', not 'it only works in hindsight'.

investigations.title: Facts sheet: prompts, what was already tried, and the second corpus

report.headline: The LLMs pick one label from a closed list of 424 IMDRF paths, sorted alphabetically. All 46 rare codes are in that list. The list gives no definitions, frequencies or device information, and it has no option for "no problem", "insufficient information" or "none of these". The pool build removed the IMDRF A24-A27 codes and every report with more than one code, and the label list leaves out 47 codes on purpose, among them common parent codes such as "Battery Problem" (5,946 reports in 2026). Several attractor codes are the only listed child under a parent that is hidden or missing from the list, so the closed list itself pushes answers toward them. Every coder the repo has run makes thousands of false rare answers a year when used zero-shot: Fable, Opus (with and without reasoning), Sonnet, Haiku, gpt-oss, Qwen 27B and 4B, and Gemma. The best two are Opus with reasoning at about 3,000 and Fable at about 5,600, against 4,100 for plain Opus. Three things cut false rare answers by an order of magnitude, all by narrowing or anchoring the candidate list: showing only the labels of the 10 nearest neighbours, letting the encoder vet the LLM's answer, and fine-tuning. Each also loses rare-code recall. An NONE_OF_THESE option plus a self-reported novelty score did not separate right from false rare answers. The SDR aircraft corpus has no natural-proportion sample. Reweighting its balanced test (a method I checked on MAUDE, where it agrees within 1.1-1.5x) shows the same pattern, milder: zero-shot rare answers are right only 6-10% of the time there, against 1-2% on MAUDE. SDR's rare base rate is 8x higher (0.68% vs 0.083%), half its listed codes are rare, and its false rare answers also land on template words ("NOT GROUNDED", "NON ISSUE"). My loader reproduces the encoder 2026 figures exactly (32 right / 166 false, accuracy 0.6365).

leads: Add the missing 'way out' labels and rerun zero-shot on the 2026 natural sample: the A24-A27 'no problem identified / insufficient information' codes and the hidden parents (Battery Problem, Connection Problem), or an explicit 'only the parent is clear' instruction. This needs a new LLM run: about 5,785 requests on the local GPU (Qwen/Gemma; the 2026nat zero-shot runs took about 2.7 and 4.3 hours) or about $5-10 for Opus by batch. It tests whether the attractor codes are an artefact of the closed list.

Encoder top-k shortlist in the prompt (the LLM picks among the encoder's top 10-20 plus all rare codes that pass a gate), or the CPU-only gate already measured here: freeze k on 2025, then apply to 2026 once. The CPU gate needs nothing new. A shortlist prompt needs a local GPU run.

Code-level counting instead of report-level: estimate each rare code's yearly count, or detect that the code appeared at all, by aggregating LLM rare answers per code with a per-(coder, code) false-answer rate learned on 2024val/2025nat. Saerens-style count correction per code needs CPU only. This may be the better problem: surveillance wants to know which rare modes appeared, not a label on every report.

Show each rare code's own training reports, or its definition, at decision time only for reports where an LLM proposes that rare code: a pairwise check, as in rare_verify, but with permission to say 'neither' and with the 2026 template families grouped. Needs API credit (about $1-3 per 400 checks with Opus) or local GPU.

Group template families before counting: near-identical manufacturer narratives (pacemaker battery, insulin pump reset) drive about 1,600 false a year each. Clustering 2026 texts by TF-IDF or MinHash and checking each cluster once is CPU only and could change the false counts a lot. The cached texts are in scratch cache_maude.pkl (items26).

On 2024 data the screen removes about 83-92% of false zero-shot rare answers but keeps only about 48% of true rare items.

surprises: The label list gives the LLM no way out. 'No problem identified / insufficient information' codes were removed with their reports, and 47 codes are hidden, including the common parents 'Battery Problem' and 'Connection Problem'.
