checks.claim: Encoder top-k gate with k=3 (the largest k with 0 sampled false on 2025): 2026 Qwen 67/330 (2), Gemma 67/170 (1), Opus 68/495 (3), accuracy about 0.636; 2025 Qwen 88/3.9, Gemma 89/4.9, Opus 87/2.0.
checks.detail: Measured with my own implementation: the encoder answer, replaced by the zero-shot rare answer when that code is in the encoder's top k. The numbers match exactly. k=5 has 1 sampled false in 2025, so k=3 really is the largest zero-false k. The rule is mechanical and can be written from 2025 alone, but they admit they wrote it after seeing 2026. Caveat: the 2026 false counts are 166 encoder false plus 0-2 extra sampled reports (each about 164 a year), so beyond the encoder's own false answers the gate adds 2 sampled (Opus), 1 (Qwen) and only 4.4 from the stratum (Gemma). Its false cost is essentially unmeasured at this resolution. The right-answer gain (+35-36 a year over the encoder) comes from the census and is solid.

checks.claim: Model comparison on the 2025 balanced test reweighted to 2025 proportions: plain Opus about 4,100 false a year, Opus with reasoning about 3,000, Fable 5,600; neighbour labels alone cut Qwen from 14,476 to 1,253.
checks.detail: Their file variants_maude.json shows Opus 31 sampled false and Opus-high 31 sampled false. The 4,072 vs 2,979 difference therefore comes only from which codes those 31 items happen to carry. 'Reasoning helps somewhat' is not supported. The natural 2025 sample I measured gives plain Opus 6,698 (35 sampled), not about 4,100, so the reweighted figure is about 1.6x low. The labels-only effect (27 sampled false vs 108) is large enough to survive that noise.

corrections: A24-A27 removal: only the top-level codes 2993/3189/3190/3191 (and 2203/2204) were removed. A2501 'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action' is a kept child of A25, which is why it ends up as the only listed code under 'No Apparent Adverse Event'.
Plain Opus zero-shot 2025 is 175 right / 6,698 false a year (35 sampled) on the natural sample, not about 4,100. The 4,072 is the reweighted balanced-test estimate.
'Reasoning helps somewhat' (Opus-high 2,979 vs Opus 4,072) is not supported: both rest on 31 sampled false items, and the difference is pure weighting.
The k=3 encoder gate's 2026 false counts are the encoder's own 166 plus 1-2 sampled reports at most. They show the gate adds few false answers at this resolution, not a measured 170-495.
check.net: Everything I recomputed on MAUDE matches exactly: the loader sanity figures, the prompt facts (424 alphabetical labels, all 46 rare codes listed, 47 hidden at every 10th rank, no abstain option), the Opus parse counts, the hidden-parent counts, the 51,153 unlisted 2026 reports, the encoder-rank separation and the k=3 gate. Two corrections. The A24-A27 removal kept the child A2501, and that is what makes 'Prophylactic removal' an orphan attractor. The cross-model comparison rests on reweighted balanced tests with about 30 sampled false items: it supports the ordering only roughly, it does not show that reasoning helps, and it understates plain Opus 2025 (6,698 natural vs 4,072 reweighted). The conclusion that the closed list (hidden parents, removed no-problem codes) pushes answers onto attractors is a well-grounded hypothesis, but it is not shown: no run with those labels restored exists. The finding that narrowing or anchoring the candidates (neighbour labels, encoder top-k) cuts false rare answers by about 10x while losing recall follows from the numbers. I did not recheck the SDR figures, prompt-token medians, the product-code screen, the novelty prompt or the LoRA figures. Scripts and outputs are in my scratch folder.

investigations.title: What others do about LLMs over-naming rare labels

report.headline: Published work describes the same failure the project sees, from the other side. Zero-shot and in-context LLM classifiers carry a label marginal p(y) of their own that does not match the data (Zhao 2021; Fei 2023; Jiang 2023; Reif & Schwartz 2024). Most papers report this as a lean toward head or early-listed labels. Here the data prior is extremely skewed, so a flatter LLM marginal shows up as rare codes named far too often. Every published correction (contextual, batch, domain-context, prototypical, prior matching, PMI) either needs log-probabilities or uses the answer frequencies, which reduces to Saerens/EM prior correction. The project has already tried that, and no paper tests any of these methods at a prevalence near 1 in 1,000. Screening arithmetic (measured from the brief's numbers) explains why this is hard rather than an LLM quirk. At prevalence 1/1,198, 50% precision at 30% recall allows at most 166 false rare answers a year, a false-alarm rate of 2.5e-4. The best Opus zero-shot rate is 1.0e-2 and the encoder's is 2.5e-4. The uniform draw of 3,974 reports cannot check that level: 0 sampled false answers still fits up to about 614 a year (95% upper bound). The literature points to changing the problem rather than tuning the coder. Options are a shortlist-then-verify or generate-then-verify pipeline that feeds a human review queue (selective prediction); per-group prevalence estimation (quantification) instead of per-report labels; and an audit of how much "false" is filing convention. The Motzfeldt et al. 2025 split (LLM best on rare codes, fine-tuned models best on frequent codes) is confirmed. The Eng et al. 2026 paper does not state a routing rule in its abstract.

findings.claim: Zero-shot and in-context LLM classifiers have a label prior of their own that is not the data prior. Published corrections estimate that prior and divide it out.
findings.evidence: Calibrate Before Use (Zhao, Wallace, Feng, Klein, Singh; ICML 2021; https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.09690): content-free input such as 'N/A' is pushed to uniform. Mitigating Label Biases for In-context Learning (Fei, Hou, Chen, Bosselut; ACL 2023; https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19148): vanilla, context and domain label bias, corrected with random in-domain words. Batch Calibration (Zhou, Wan, Proleev, Mincu, Chen, Heller, Roy; ICLR 2024; https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17249): prior estimated from the test batch. Prototypical Calibration (Han, Hao, Dong, Sun, Wei; arXiv 2022; https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10183): GMM clusters matched to labels. Mitigating Word Bias in Zero-shot Prompt-based Classifiers (Liusie, Manakul, Gales; Findings IJCNLP-AACL 2023; https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.04992): prior matching to a uniform class prior using unlabelled data. Generative Calibration for In-context Learning (Jiang, Zhang, Liu, Zhao, Liu; Findings EMNLP 2023; https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10266): frames the problem as label shift (good p(x|y), wrong p(y)) and estimates p(y) by Monte Carlo sampling. Surface Form Competition (Holtzman et al.; EMNLP 2021; https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08315): domain-conditional PMI. Beyond Performance: Quantifying and Mitigating Label Bias in LLMs (Reif, Schwartz; NAACL 2024; https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.378): substantial label bias in 10 LLMs across 279 tasks. All test sets have few classes (mostly 2 to about 100). None tests a 471-label long tail or a prevalence near 1e-3.
findings.reproduce: pages opened via WebFetch/WebSearch; URLs listed

findings.claim: Most published label-bias results show LLMs favoring early-listed or frequent labels. Accuracy also drops as the label list grows. The project's prompt lists 471 codes alphabetically, so position effects are plausible contributors to the attractor codes. This is untested here.
findings.evidence: Primacy Effect of ChatGPT (Wang, Cai, Chen, Liang, Hooi; EMNLP 2023 short; https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13206): sensitive to label order, prefers early labels. Serial Position Effects of LLMs (Guo, Vosoughi; arXiv 2024; https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15981): primacy and recency effects are widespread. Mitigating Boundary Ambiguity and Inherent Bias for Text Classification in the Era of LLMs (Lu et al.; arXiv 2024; https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07001): gpt-3.5-turbo zero-shot 32.51% with 60 categories vs 94.29% with 2; reduce-then-compare gives a 54.1% relative gain. These numbers come from a search summary of the paper; I opened the abstract page only through the search result.
findings.reproduce: literature; CPU test proposed in leads

findings.claim: Very-many-label LLM classification in published work almost always shortlists candidates first (retriever or fine-tuned model), then has the LLM rerank or choose. None reports rare-label precision at natural proportions.
findings.evidence: ICXML (Zhu, Zamani; Findings NAACL 2024; https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09649): generate candidates, then rerank, on LF-Amazon-131K and LF-WikiSeeAlso-320K. In-Context Learning for Extreme Multi-Label Classification / Infer-Retrieve-Rank (D'Oosterlinck, Khattab, Remy, Demeester, Develder, Potts; arXiv 2024; https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12178): thousands of classes. LLMs are good medical coders, if provided with tools (Kwan; arXiv 2024; https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12849): ColBERT top-15, then LLM rerank, 100% on 100 single-term inputs vs 6% for vanilla GPT-3.5. Automated clinical coding using off-the-shelf LLMs (Boyle et al.; NeurIPS 2023 DGM4H workshop; https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06552): ICD tree search, macro-F1 0.225 vs PLM-ICD 0.216 on CodiEsp.

findings.claim: Clinical coding with LLMs: plain prompting is poor and over-codes; verification and evidence-grounding steps help. The rare→LLM / frequent→fine-tuned split is stated by Motzfeldt et al. but not, as far as the abstract shows, by Eng et al.
findings.evidence: LLMs Are Poor Medical Coders (Soroush et al.; NEJM AI 2024; DOI 10.1056/AIdbp2300040): GPT-4 exact match ICD-10-CM 33.9%. Code Like Humans (Motzfeldt, Edin, Christensen, Hardmeier, Maaløe, Rogers; Findings EMNLP 2025; https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05378) abstract: 'best performance to date on rare diagnosis codes' and fine-tuned classifiers 'retain an advantage for high-frequency codes'. Understanding the Limits of Agentic ICD Coding (Eng, Cao, Chen, Mao, Jiang; arXiv 2609.13806, listed as EMNLP 2026 main): neural classifiers drop 0.43 micro-F1 on rare codes, workflow systems do well on rare codes but near zero on injury codes; the abstract states no routing rule. Toward Reliable Clinical Coding with LMs: Verification and Lightweight Adaptation (Yuan, Shing, Strong, Shivade; arXiv 2510.07629, EMNLP 2025 Industry per a search snippet): hierarchical near-misses are a substantial share of failures; verification helps; the search summary says the models over-code. MedCodER (Baksi et al.; arXiv 2409.15368, NAACL 2025 industry): extract evidence, retrieve, rerank, micro-F1 0.60-0.62. Self-Verification Improves Few-Shot Clinical IE (Gero et al.; ICML 2023 IMLH workshop; https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00024): the LLM cites provenance and checks its own output. None reports rare-code precision at a base rate near 1e-3.

findings.claim: Published work on MAUDE/IMDRF is thin and agrees that agreement with filed codes falls sharply at finer levels. I found no paper that codes MAUDE to the full IMDRF Annex A leaf with a fine-tuned model plus LLMs at natural proportions.
findings.evidence: A Framework for LLM-Guided and ISO 5338-Aligned Data Engineering in Medical Device Adverse Event Reporting (Muaz, Janjua, Loughran, St John Lynch; AIAI 2026; https://eprints.dkit.ie/id/eprint/1049/): of 10,000 MAUDE events, 1,728 device-problem records kept where human and LLM agree at level 2; GPT-OSS-120B consensus 59.49% at level 1 and 23.04% at level 3. Leveraging LLMs to Understand Narratives in MAUDE Reports (Shi, Gong; Stud Health Technol Inform vol 323, DOI 10.3233/SHTI250076): GPT-4-turbo on endoscopic-clip narratives, no comparable metrics. MedDRA: ALIGN (arXiv 2411.13163) and an ALTA 2025 hybrid MedDRA system (aclanthology 2025.alta-main.16) were seen only in search snippets and not opened, so they are not relied on.

findings.claim: Registry codes as the answer key: published work shows that a fair share of 'errors' can be the key's fault. FDA says MAUDE codes are chosen by the submitter, a report can carry several problem codes, and follow-up reports change the record.
findings.evidence: Experimental Evaluation and Development of a Silver-Standard for the MIMIC-III Clinical Coding Dataset (Searle, Ibrahim, Dobson; BioNLP 2020; https://aclanthology.org/2020.bionlp-1.8): the most frequent codes are under-coded by up to 35%. Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets (Northcutt, Athalye, Mueller; NeurIPS 2021 D&B; https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14749): at least 3.3% average test-label error, enough to flip model rankings. FDA MAUDE page (https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/mandatory-reporting-requirements-manufacturers-importers-and-device-user-facilities/manufacturer-and-user-facility-device-experience-database-maude): submitters choose codes; data are not meant for rates. The project's 'potential high impedance within the battery' template example fits this.

findings.claim: Counting instead of classifying is an established field (quantification). Adjusted classify-and-count, BBSE, and EM prior estimation give unbiased prevalence even from a biased classifier. At prevalence near 1e-3 per group, their variance is the problem, and Rogan-Gladen can go negative when the apparent rate is below 1 - specificity.
findings.evidence: Detecting and Correcting for Label Shift with Black Box Predictors (Lipton, Wang, Smola; ICML 2018; https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03916). Adjusting the Outputs of a Classifier to New a Priori Probabilities (Saerens, Latinne, Decaestecker; Neural Computation 14(1) 2002; DOI 10.1162/089976602753284446). Maximum Likelihood with Bias-Corrected Calibration is Hard-To-Beat at Label Shift Adaptation (Alexandari, Kundaje, Shrikumar; ICML 2020; https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.06852): EM plus class-wise bias calibration beats BBSE/RLLS. Quantifying counts and costs via classification (Forman; Data Min Knowl Disc 17(2) 2008, seen as a library record only). Learning to Quantify (Esuli, Fabris, Moreo, Sebastiani; Springer 2023, open access; DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-20467-8). Estimating prevalence from the results of a screening test (Rogan, Gladen; Am J Epidemiol 107(1) 1978; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/623091/). Estimating prevalence with precision and accuracy (Igiraneza, Fraser, Hinch; arXiv 2507.06061): Bayesian quantifier with intervals; its abstract says nothing specific about low prevalence. I found no quantification benchmark at prevalence of 1e-3 or below.

findings.claim: Signal detection in pharmacovigilance treats miscoding as a known bias. In the sources found, the tolerance is built into how signals are read, not into fixing the classifier.
findings.evidence: Search surfaced Khouri et al. 2021 (Frontiers in Pharmacology, PMC8193489): disproportionality results vary across models for 60% of drug-event pairs. A Drug Safety paper listing misclassification by miscoding as a bias source was seen only in a snippet and not opened. I found no study that quantifies how much classifier noise a disproportionality signal tolerates.

findings.claim: Screening arithmetic at 2026 prevalence: the precision the current coders reach is set by their false-alarm rate on ordinary reports. 50% precision at 30% recall needs at most 166 false a year (false-alarm rate 2.5e-4), which only the encoder meets, and the encoder reaches 5.8% recall.
findings.evidence: Prevalence 552/661,160 = 8.35e-4 (1 in 1,198). False-alarm rate per 1,000 ordinary reports, with precision in brackets: encoder 0.25 (0.162); zs Qwen 22.2 (0.009), Gemma 21.9 (0.011), Opus 10.1 (0.023); rag 4.1/3.4/4.6 (0.028/0.040/0.030); Opus Saerens 1.07 (0.076); Qwen Saerens 0.005 (0.90, recall 0.049); Opus rules 0.575 (0.132) and 1.32 (0.097). Maximum false a year for a target: recall 0.1 at precision 0.5 allows 55; recall 0.3 at precision 0.5 allows 166; recall 0.5 at precision 0.8 allows 69. Inputs are the brief's yearly numbers, divided by 660,608 non-rare reports. The yearly false counts include stratum rows, so this rate is approximate.
findings.reproduce: screening_arithmetic.py in the scratch folder, run with the given Python pattern; output in screening_arithmetic.txt/.json

findings.claim: The uniform draw cannot check precision targets at this prevalence. With 3,974 uniform reports, one sampled false answer stands for about 166 a year with a 95% interval of 4 to 927. Zero sampled false still fits up to 614 a year (exact Poisson), or 499 by the rule of three. Estimating a false-alarm rate of 1e-3 to ±25% needs about 61,000 uniform reports; a rate of 1e-4 to ±50% needs about 154,000.
findings.evidence: Exact Poisson 95% CIs scaled by 661,160/3,974 = 166.4 (the brief's 164 applies to frequent-code rows only): 0 → [0, 614]; 1 → [4, 927]; 5 → [270, 1,941]; 88 → [11,742, 18,038]. n needed = (1.96/r)^2 (1-f)/f. Example Clopper-Pearson interval for flag precision 58/438: [0.102, 0.168]; for 2/23: [0.011, 0.28].

findings.claim: Selective prediction and conformal methods with many classes exist, but their guarantees concern coverage or risk across classes, not precision on 1-5-example classes. They need a score (log-probabilities or repeated sampling) that the stored outputs lack.
findings.evidence: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks (Geifman, El-Yaniv; NeurIPS 2017; https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08500): risk-coverage with a guaranteed risk. Class-Conditional Conformal Prediction with Many Classes (Ding, Angelopoulos, Bates, Jordan, Tibshirani; NeurIPS 2023; https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/cb931eddd563f8d473c355518ce8601c-Abstract.html): pools classes with similar scores because per-class calibration fails with few examples. API Is Enough: Conformal Prediction for LLMs Without Logit-Access (Su, Luo, Wang, Cheng; Findings EMNLP 2024; https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01216): sample frequency plus semantic similarity as the score, which needs many samples per report.

findings.claim: Base-rate arithmetic from intrusion detection carries over directly: the false-alarm rate, not the detection rate, limits usefulness when positives are this rare.
findings.evidence: The Base-Rate Fallacy and the Difficulty of Intrusion Detection (Axelsson; ACM TISSEC 3(3) 2000; DOI 10.1145/357830.357849). The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot ... on Imbalanced Datasets (Saito, Rehmsmeier; PLoS ONE 2015; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4349800).

leads: PROMISING 1. Shortlist-then-verify with an admissibility gate. Let the LLM name a rare code only if that code is among the encoder's top-k or the 10 retrieval neighbours' codes, then run a verification prompt ('does this report support code X over its nearest frequent sibling? quote the evidence'). Literature: ICXML, Infer-Retrieve-Rank, Kwan 2024, MedCodER, Yuan 2025 verification, Gero 2023. Needs: CPU on stored outputs for the gate alone, using encoder top-k from runs/maude_encprobs and neighbors_full.json; choose k on 2024val/2025nat. Local GPU for the verification prompt on gated candidates only, which is small. No published evidence at a prevalence near 1e-3.

PROMISING 2. Reframe as a review queue (selective prediction) and measure it properly. The output is a short ranked list of rare-code candidates for a human, judged by precision of flags and by rare reports surfaced per 100 reviewed. Arithmetic shows precision is capped by the false-alarm rate, and the 3,974-report uniform draw cannot check rates below about 1.5e-4 per report. Two-phase evaluation: run the cheap stage (encoder, local GPU about once) over all 661k 2026 reports, run LLMs only on flagged reports, and audit a random sample of flags. That measures precision directly without a 60k+ uniform draw. Needs: local GPU (encoder over the full pool, LLM on flags) plus human audit time.

PROMISING 3. Count instead of classify, at the level of rare-code groups (IMDRF level 1/2 families or all rare codes pooled), not per code. Use EM/Saerens prior estimation (Alexandari 2020: hard to beat) or adjusted classify-and-count with confusion rates estimated on 2025nat, and report intervals. Needs: CPU on stored outputs. Caveat: per-code ACC at a false-alarm rate of 1e-3 vs prevalence of 1e-5 per code will be dominated by variance or go negative (Rogan-Gladen); test on 2025 with 2024 confusion first.

PROMISING 4. Audit the key. Have a human read a stratified sample of 'false' rare answers, especially attractor codes and manufacturer templates, and label each as wrong code, defensible alternative (near-miss in the IMDRF hierarchy), or filing convention. Also score at IMDRF level 2 as Muaz et al. 2026 and Yuan et al. 2025 do. Searle 2020 found up to 35% under-coding in MIMIC. Needs: CPU to draw the sample; human time (about 100-200 reports).

PROMISING 5. Prior correction from answer frequencies, done per LLM and per prompt, without logprobs. Estimate the LLM's own label marginal on 2024val (natural proportions) from its answer counts, then apply a Saerens/generative-calibration style reweight, or divide by the LLM's answer-rate ratio to the data prior. Also test whether false-rare rate per code correlates with its position in the alphabetical prompt list (primacy, per Wang 2023 / Guo 2024). If it does, shuffled-order re-prompting is a cheap fix. Needs: CPU on stored outputs for the analysis; local GPU only to re-prompt with shuffled order.

DEAD END 1. The logit-based calibration family (contextual, batch, domain-context, prototypical calibration, prior matching, PMI) as published. It needs per-label probabilities over 471 multi-token labels, which the stored outputs lack and which are costly to get by scoring all labels. It was tested only on few-class tasks. Its answer-frequency version reduces to Saerens prior correction, already tried (Opus 58/707, Qwen 27/3), so remaining headroom looks small.

DEAD END 2. Class-conditional conformal or selective-risk guarantees for the 46 rare codes. With 1-5 training examples per code and 0.083% prevalence, per-class calibration sets do not exist, and clustered conformal (Ding 2023) pools codes so the guarantee no longer applies per rare code. Without logits it needs repeated sampling per report (Su 2024), which is GPU/API-heavy. Coverage guarantees also do not control precision, which is the binding constraint here.

Also worth noting, lower priority: an ICD-style agentic or hierarchy-walking coder (Boyle 2023 tree search; Motzfeldt 2025 Code Like Humans) for rare codes only. Needs: many LLM calls per report (local GPU or API). Evidence is for rare-code recall and F1, not for precision at natural proportions.
caveats: Several references were confirmed through search-result summaries of their official pages rather than by opening the paper itself: Soroush 2024, Kwan 2024, Boyle 2023, MedCodER, Searle 2020, Northcutt 2021, Rogan-Gladen 1978, Axelsson 2000, Saito 2015, Alexandari 2020, Geifman 2017, Su 2024, Esuli 2023, Lu 2024, Reif & Schwartz 2024. Pages opened directly via WebFetch: Zhao 2021, Zhou 2023, Han 2022, Fei 2023, Jiang 2023, D'Oosterlinck 2024, Eng 2026, Motzfeldt 2025, Lipton 2018, Ding 2023, Muaz 2026, Shi & Gong, Igiraneza 2025, Guo 2024, Wang 2023, Yuan 2025.
Forman 2008 was seen only as a library record. MedDRA LLM papers (ALIGN, ALTA 2025) and the Drug Safety miscoding paper were seen only in snippets and are not relied on.

Venue details: Yuan et al. 2025 is listed on arXiv with no venue; a search snippet says EMNLP 2025 Industry. Prototypical Calibration has no venue on its arXiv page. Eng et al. 2026's EMNLP 2026 acceptance is taken from its arXiv comment.
The rare→LLM / frequent→fine-tuned framing is confirmed for Motzfeldt et al. 2025. For Eng et al. (2609.13806) the abstract does not state it; that would need the full text, which I did not read.

The screening arithmetic uses only the yearly numbers in the brief, not repo data, so I did not run the loader sanity check (encoder 32/166, accuracy 0.6365). Uniform weight is taken as 661,160/3,974 = 166.4; the brief's 164 is for frequent-code rows. False-alarm rates divide yearly false counts, which include stratum rows, by all non-rare reports, so they are approximate.
I found no published method evaluated at a prevalence near 1e-3 with hundreds of labels. Every claim that a method helps 'at this prevalence' is inference.
surprises: Most published label-bias work reports LLMs favoring head or early-listed labels, the opposite direction from 'over-naming rare codes'. The two fit together if the LLM's own label marginal is far flatter than the data's extreme skew: Jiang et al. 2023 frame in-context learning errors as exactly this label shift.

The only MAUDE/IMDRF LLM study found (Muaz et al., AIAI 2026) keeps only records where human and LLM codes agree, and reports level-3 agreement of 23% for GPT-OSS-120B. Leaf-level, natural-proportion MAUDE coding appears unstudied.

Arithmetic: the encoder is the only coder already at the false-alarm rate (2.5e-4 per ordinary report) that 50% precision needs, yet it finds 5.8% of rare reports. Qwen with prior correction reaches 0.90 precision at 4.9% recall. The precision-recall frontier at this prevalence is extremely steep for every coder.

checks.claim: Label-bias / calibration papers: Zhao 2021 (ICML), Fei 2023 (ACL), Zhou 2024 Batch Calibration (ICLR), Han 2022 Prototypical (arXiv), Liusie 2023 (Findings IJCNLP-AACL), Jiang 2023 Generative Calibration (Findings EMNLP), Holtzman 2021 (EMNLP), Reif & Schwartz 2024 (NAACL; 10 LLMs, 279 tasks)
checks.detail: I opened each arXiv or ACL page. Authors, years and venues match, and so does each method: 'N/A' content-free input pushed to uniform; random in-domain words; GMM clusters with bipartite matching; reweighting to a uniform prior without labels; label shift with p(y) estimated by Monte-Carlo generation; domain-conditional PMI; 10 LLMs on 279 tasks. Liusie's venue and Holtzman's EMNLP 2021 come from ACL Anthology search records, not the arXiv pages. For Batch Calibration the abstract does not say how the prior is estimated, so 'estimated from the test batch' is the investigator's paraphrase. The claim that 'none tests 471 labels or a prevalence near 1e-3' is a negative I cannot check; nothing I read contradicts it.

checks.claim: Position effects: Wang 2023 Primacy Effect (EMNLP short), Guo & Vosoughi 2024 (arXiv), Lu et al. 2024 (32.51% with 60 categories vs 94.29% with 2; 54.1% relative gain)
checks.detail: Wang and Guo are confirmed as described. For Lu et al. I read the exact sentences in the arXiv HTML: 32.51% with 60 categories, 94.29% with 2, and a 54.1% relative gain. The venue is wrong, though: the arXiv comment says ACL 2024 Findings, not a plain arXiv preprint. The step from these papers to 'the alphabetical list of 471 codes produces the attractor codes' is untested, and the investigator says so.

checks.claim: Shortlist-then-rerank papers: ICXML (Findings NAACL 2024; LF-Amazon-131K, LF-WikiSeeAlso-320K), Infer-Retrieve-Rank (arXiv 2024), Kwan 2024 (ColBERT top-15; 100% vs 6% on 100 terms), Boyle 2023 (NeurIPS DGM4H; macro-F1 0.225 vs PLM-ICD 0.216 on CodiEsp)
checks.detail: All checked against the papers' own pages and HTML full texts. ICXML is in the ACL Anthology as 2024.findings-naacl.134; Table 1 lists 131,073 and 312,330 labels. Kwan: ColBERT-V2 with k=15, 100% vs 6% on 100 single-term conditions. Boyle: 0.225 vs 0.216 in Table 1. The abstract says 'hierarchical search'; 'tree search' appears in the paper's text.

checks.claim: Clinical coding: Soroush 2024 NEJM AI (GPT-4 ICD-10-CM exact match 33.9%), Motzfeldt 2025 (Findings EMNLP; rare-code quote), Eng 2026 (EMNLP 2026 main; 0.43 micro-F1; no routing rule), Yuan 2025 (verification; over-codes), MedCodER (NAACL 2025 industry; 0.60-0.62), Gero 2023 (IMLH)
checks.detail: Motzfeldt: both abstract quotes confirmed verbatim. Eng: the abstract gives the 0.43 as a 'gap between rare and common codes' for neural classifiers, not as a drop. 'Near zero on injury codes' is confirmed, and there is no routing rule in the abstract. Yuan: confirmed as EMNLP 2025 Industry (ACL Anthology 2025.emnlp-industry.12), and the near-miss and verification claims hold. 'Over-codes' is not in the abstract and is unconfirmed. MedCodER: the arXiv v1 reports 0.60 and the NAACL 2025 Industry version reports 0.62 (from a search summary), so the range holds. Gero: confirmed (IMLH 2023). check.net: The references hold up. I opened or looked up all of them, and none is invented. The errors are minor: one venue is understated (Lu 2024 is ACL Findings), one number is reworded (Eng's 0.43 is a gap, not a drop), one paraphrase is unconfirmed (Yuan 'over-codes'), the Soroush DOI could not be checked, and Northcutt's ranking flips are hypothetical. I recomputed all of the screening arithmetic and every number matches. The arithmetic supports the main conclusion that, at a prevalence of 1 in 1,198, the false-alarm rate on ordinary reports caps precision and the 3,974-report uniform draw cannot verify any useful target. Two points go further than the numbers allow. First, the data cannot show that the encoder 'meets' the 2.5e-4 target: it sits at 166 against 165.6 allowed, from one sampled false answer. Second, lead 2 understates the sampling limit; the draw only bounds the rate at about 9e-4, not 1.5e-4. The causal story (a flatter LLM label marginal, prompt-order primacy) and 'all corrections reduce to Saerens, already tried' are inference, not shown. The second is too strong, because answer-count BBSE and sampling-based generative calibration are separate options that do not need logprobs. The pointers to reframing (review queue with two-phase audit, group-level quantification, auditing the key) follow reasonably, but no source tests them at this prevalence.

investigations.title: Base-rate arithmetic, measurement resolution and counting-level alternatives

report.headline: The base rate makes the target very hard, though not impossible in principle. With 552 rare-code reports among 661,160, a coder needs a false-alarm rate of about 1 in 12,000 ordinary reports to reach 50% precision at 10% recall, and about 1 in 2,400 to reach 50% precision at 50% recall. The zero-shot LLMs put a false rare code on 1 in 100 ordinary reports (Opus) or 1 in 45 (Qwen, Gemma), so they are 40 to 100 times too loose. The rules that are already that strict (encoder and LLM agreeing; prior-corrected Qwen) only reach 4-5% recall. A second-stage checker would need a positive likelihood ratio of about 31-43 (for example sensitivity 0.39-0.65 with specificity 0.985-0.991 starting from Opus zero-shot). The best checker built so far reached about 4.5, and Opus's own second look reached 1.08. The uniform draw of 3,974 reports cannot measure the regime that matters: seeing zero false answers still allows up to about 498 a year (sampled 0, 95% bound), which is more than the whole false budget of a 50%-precision rule at any recall up to 50%. A cheap gate fixes much of the measurement problem: send a report to the LLM only when the encoder puts enough probability on rare codes, with the threshold set on 2025. That flags about 7% of reports, still holds 304 of the 552 rare reports, cuts Opus's false answers from 6,665 to 1,526 a year (9 sampled) while keeping 123 of its 154 right ones, and makes the measurement 14 times cheaper (about 1,382 gated reports certify at most 100 false a year, against 19,806 uniform). Counting per code does not get around the problem. Corrected counts are usually worse than raw counts, because per-code false-alarm counts rest on 0-25 sampled reports and swing 2-3x between years. A tenfold jump in an attractor code is buried, a jump in a quiet code shows up only if the coder actually names that code, and for some codes no coder ever names it right.

findings.claim: The base-rate map: the false-alarm rate per ordinary report (660,608 of them) that each precision/recall target allows.
Where every existing coder sits on that map (2026): the LLM coders are 40-100 times too loose, and the strict rules have recall of 5% or less.

Recall / false-alarm rate on ordinary reports / precision [sampled false]:
- Opus zs: 0.279 / 1 in 100 / 0.023 [40]
- Qwen zs: 0.237 / 1 in 45 / 0.009 [88]
- Gemma zs: 0.286 / 1 in 46 / 0.011 [87]
- rag: 0.14-0.17 / 1 in 222-300 / 0.03-0.04 [13-18]
- zs_and_rag: 0.12-0.15 / 1 in 267-394 / 0.03-0.04 [10-15]
- selector: 0.16-0.23 / 1 in 132-173 [23-30]
- Opus prior-corrected: 0.105 / 1 in 984 / 0.076 [4]

findings.claim: A second-stage checker would need a positive likelihood ratio of about 31-43. The checkers tried so far reached 1.1-4.5.

From Opus zs (154 / 6,665; prior odds 0.023):
- keep 60 right: sensitivity >= 0.39, specificity >= 0.991
- keep 100 right: sensitivity >= 0.65, specificity >= 0.985
- likelihood ratio needed: 43
From zs_and_rag (80 / 2,516): keep 60 needs sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.976 (likelihood ratio 31.5); keep 100 is impossible (needs sensitivity 1.25).
From the selector's rare picks (125 / 3,856): keep 60 needs 0.48 / 0.984; keep 100 needs 0.80 / 0.974.
Achieved on the selector's rare picks (results/rare_check/metrics_2026*.json):
- checker v1: sensitivity 0.584, specificity 0.870, likelihood ratio 4.5, precision 0.127
- checker v2 with Opus second look: 0.52 / 0.87, likelihood ratio 4.0
- Opus second-look verdict alone: 0.752 / 0.302, likelihood ratio 1.08 (94 right / 2,691 false)

findings.claim: The current uniform draw cannot resolve the precision range that matters. Zero sampled false answers still allow about 500 a year.
findings.evidence: With 0 false seen in n uniform reports, the 95% upper bound a year is 498 for n = 3,974, 198 for 10,000, 99 for 20,000, 40 for 50,000 and 20 for 100,000. Certifying at most 500 / 100 / 50 a year with zero false needs n = 3,960 / 19,806 / 39,612. To have 80% power when the true count is half the target (accept if at most 12 false are seen), n = 25,710 / 128,547 / 257,093. Today's sampled-false counts are coarse: Opus zs 40 sampled gives 6,560 a year (95% 4,687-8,933); prior-corrected Opus 4 sampled gives 656 (179-1,680); encoder 1 sampled gives 164 (4-914).

findings.claim: An encoder rare-probability gate (threshold set on 2025) cuts false answers about 4x and makes measurement about 14x cheaper. Inside the gate, precision is still only about 7.5%.
findings.evidence:
Gate: sum of encoder probability on rare codes, top 5% of the 2025 uniform draw (threshold 0.00354). Applied to 2026, it flags 6.98% of the uniform draw (about 46,149 reports a year) and 304 of the 552 rare reports.
Right / false a year inside the gate [sampled false]:
- Opus zs: 123 / 1,526 [9] (ungated 154 / 6,665 [40])
- Opus zs_and_rag: 65 / 694 [4]
- Qwen zs: 102 / 2,888 [17]
- Gemma zs: 118 / 3,036 [18]
Top 1% gate: Opus zs 75 / 845 [5]; 156 rare reports flagged.
On 2025 the same 5% gate gave Opus zs 127 / 594 [3], so in 2026 it removed fewer false answers than it did in 2025.
If accepted rare answers are restricted to the gate, the LLM runs only on gated reports and false answers are counted exactly: certifying at most 500 / 100 / 50 false a year needs 275 / 1,382 / 2,764 gated reports (vs 3,960 / 19,806 / 39,612 uniform). A checker inside the gate, starting from 123 / 1,526 and keeping 60 at P50, needs sensitivity 0.49 and specificity 0.961 (likelihood ratio about 12), which is still about 3x past the best checker so far.

Seconds per report (2026 natural sample; range across sets in brackets; a cold, uncached prompt costs 4.5-7 s):

- Gemma rag: 1.34 [1.34-2.93]

- Qwen rag: 2.9 / 14.5 / 191
- Gemma zs: 2.7 / 13.6 / 179

findings.claim: Adjusted classify-and-count (hit rate pooled over rare codes on 2025, per-code false-alarm rate from 2025) does not make per-code counts more accurate, and its uncertainty is thousands of reports a year per code.
findings.evidence:
Median absolute error per rare code, raw vs corrected:
- Opus zs: 5.5 vs 5.1
- Opus rag: 5.0 vs 10.5
- Qwen zs: 12.6 vs 100.6
- Gemma zs: 6.8 vs 14.1
Corrected totals over the 46 codes are 733-20,365 against a true 552.
Median 90% interval width per code a year, counting only the 2025 calibration noise: 1,683 (Opus zs) to 4,878 (encoder). The true counts are 1-27. Only 2-35% of codes have their true count inside the interval, so the intervals are also miscalibrated.
Cause: false-alarm counts rest on 0-25 sampled reports (one sampled report = 189.5 a year in 2025, 164 in 2026) and drift between years. Opus zs on Prophylactic removal: 1,898 [10] -> 497 [3]; Failure to Reset: 1,328 [7] -> 2,463 [15]; Battery Problem: High Impedance: 570 [3] -> 1,643 [10].

findings.claim: Detecting a tenfold jump k -> 10k with measured rates (examples chosen on 2025 only): attractor codes are buried, some codes are invisible to every coder, and quiet codes show only if the coder names them and the false-alarm rate is measured well.
findings.evidence:
Attractor, Prophylactic removal (k = 24 in 2025, 27 in 2026):
- LLM zs: rise of 45-108 against 1,898-4,767 false a year with year-to-year swings of 700-1,700. z = 1.0-1.6 against Poisson noise alone, about 0 once drift is counted.
- Encoder: hit 2/24, 0 false sampled. z = 12.7 nominal but 0.8 if its false count sits at the zero-sample upper bound.
Battery Problem: High Impedance and Failure to Reset (enc / Qwen / Gemma): hit 0/2 or 0/5. No rise is possible, and the LLM counts (570-2,628 a year) are template false alarms.
Quiet code, Aborted Charge (15 -> 150): Opus zs and rag hit 5/15 with 0 false sampled. The rise of 45 gives z = 20 nominal, 2.0 at the false upper bound.
Quiet code, Misassembly During Maintenance/Repair (17 -> 170): only the encoder ever names it (5/17); every LLM is 0/17.

findings.claim: What is unavoidable, what is only unmeasured, and what looks achievable.
findings.evidence:
Unavoidable (arithmetic): at a prevalence of 8.3e-4, precision >= 50% needs a per-ordinary-report false-alarm rate of 8e-5 to 4e-4 for recall of 10-50%. Any checker needs a likelihood ratio of about 30-40 on the LLM's rare answers. With these three coders recall cannot exceed 150-176/552 (27-32%).
Only unmeasured: the false count of every strict rule (0-4 sampled false, each worth 164 a year), every per-code false-alarm rate, and whether a quiet code's rise would show.
Achievable, partly measured: gating the LLM with the encoder's rare probability keeps about 80% of its right rare answers, cuts false 4x, and turns the false count into an exact census of about 46k reports a year (8-13 GPU-hours). That makes P >= 50% rules testable for about 1.4k-2.8k LLM calls. Reaching P50 still needs a better checker or rule inside the gate, and none of the measured ones gets there.

leads: Gated rerun (GPU, user's go-ahead needed): run Qwen or Gemma zs and rag on all 2025 reports where the encoder's rare probability is at least 0.00354 (about 7% of the year, about 50k reports, 8-19 GPU-hours). Re-fit and screen rules on that census, then do the same for 2026. This removes the 164-per-sampled-report coarseness for any rule that accepts LLM rare answers only inside the gate.

Encoder probabilities for the whole year (CPU, slow, or GPU, short): the gate needs the encoder on all 661,160 2026 reports, plus 2025. Right now the gate share is estimated from the 3,974-report uniform draw (7% flagged, 277 sampled).

Per-code accept list built on the gated 2025 census (CPU after the rerun): keep a (coder, code) pair only when its census false count is below a budget. This replaces the current screens, which rest on 0-3 sampled false per code.

Template de-duplication before counting (CPU): false answers pile onto near-identical manufacturer texts (Battery High Impedance: the same 3 -> 10 sampled reports in every LLM). Collapse near-duplicate texts per manufacturer and code each cluster once, then measure how much of the 1,643-a-year false count is a handful of templates.

Reframe the target (human decision): in MAUDE the filed code is the gold and is free, so watching rare modes by filed code costs nothing. A more useful LLM job may be flagging reports whose text points to a different rare mode than the filed one, a mis-filing screen whose precision can be audited per code. Inferred, not tested.

Checker target inside the gate (API or GPU): with 123 right / 1,526 false in the gate, a pairwise second look needs a likelihood ratio of about 12, not 43. Re-test the existing Opus second-look prompt on gated rare answers only (a few hundred calls).
caveats: All yearly false counts outside the census strata come from the 3,974-report uniform draw: one sampled report stands for 164 a year in 2026 and 189.5 in 2025. Sampled counts are given next to yearly counts, and a strict rule's false count (0-4 sampled) is barely measured.

The gate threshold comes from the 2025 uniform draw. I report a grid of gates (1-20%) and picked none of them using 2026. The suggested 5% gate rests on its 2025 numbers, and in 2026 it removed fewer false answers than in 2025 (1,526 vs 594).

Corrected counts use a hit rate pooled over all rare codes. Per-code hit rates differ a lot (0/17 to 12/24), which accounts for part of the bad correction. A per-code hit rate would rest on 1-24 reports a code.

The Monte Carlo intervals put a Gamma(sampled + 1) distribution on false counts, which is conservative (wide) when 0 false were sampled. Detection z-values are given at the observed false count and at the zero-sample upper bound (about +492 a year). They assume Poisson noise plus the observed 2025-2026 change, which itself includes sampling noise.
In the 2025 vs 2026 comparison the year sizes differ (762,360 vs 661,160 reports). False-alarm rates were scaled per report.
The seconds per report are wall time per request on a GPU the user also uses for other work (Gemma 2025nat at 2.4 s looks slowed down). No dollar costs were computed.
The checker requirements take the 2026 counts (154/6,665 etc.) as given. Those counts carry their own sampling error: Opus zs false a year 95% 4,687-8,933 from 40 sampled.
surprises: Of the ~500 false a year that zero false in the current 3,974-report draw still allows, almost all would land on ordinary reports. That allowance alone exceeds the whole false budget of a 50%-precision rule at any recall up to 50%. The current design cannot confirm any such rule.
Opus's second look on the selector's rare picks is almost uninformative: likelihood ratio 1.08 (sensitivity 0.75, specificity 0.30). It picked the rare code on most false rare picks.

Battery Problem: High Impedance: no coder was right on any of its 2 reports in 2025, and every LLM (zs and rag, all three models) falsely names it on the same 3 sampled reports in 2025 and the same 10 in 2026. It looks like one template text, not model noise.

A quiet code (Misassembly During Maintenance/Repair, 17 reports in 2025) is never named by any LLM (0/17). Only the fine-tuned encoder sees it (5/17), so for counting, a code can be invisible to the LLMs rather than over-named.

The encoder's rare-probability mass is a strong ranker: 55% of rare reports (304/552) sit in the top 7% of reports and 77% (423/552) in the top 13.5%. The LLMs' false rare answers are less concentrated there (23-31% inside the 5% gate).
