checks.claim: Zero sampled false in 3,974 uniform reports still allows about 498 false a year (95%); certifying <=100 needs 19,806 uniform reports
checks.detail: Measured: -ln(0.05)/3974 x 661,160 = 498.4, and 2.996 x 661,160 / 100 = 19,806. 498 exceeds the P50 budget at R50 (276), so the statement that no P50 rule up to R50 can be confirmed with this draw follows.

checks.claim: Encoder rare-mass gate (top 5% of the 2025 uniform draw, threshold 0.00354) flags 6.98% of 2026, holds 304/552 rare reports, cuts Opus zs to 123 / 1,526 [9]; Qwen 102 / 2,888 [17], Gemma 118 / 3,036 [18]; 2025 Opus 127 / 594 [3]; top-1% gate Opus 75 / 845 [5], 156 rare
checks.detail: Measured with my own key alignment to the npz. All 9,741 / 9,831 keys were found, row probabilities sum to 1.0, and npz argmax equals the stored encoder answer on 99.4-100% of rows, so a few rows differ slightly; small effect. Threshold 0.003543 is taken from the 2025 uniform draw only. On 2026: 279 of 4,000 uniform rows flagged (6.98%), 304/552 rare reports. Gated 2026: Opus zs 123 / 1,526.0 [9], Qwen 102 / 2,887.5 [17], Gemma 118 / 3,036.3 [18], Opus zs_and_rag 65 / 693.9 [4]. Gated 2025: Opus 127 / 593.8 [3]. 1% gate: t = 0.01344, Opus 2026 75 / 844.5 [5], 156 rare. Caveats the headline glosses over: (a) the gated false counts rest on 9-18 sampled reports, so Opus's 1,526 has a rough 95% range of about 670-2,800 a year (Poisson on 9; inferred); (b) the cut was 11x on 2025 but only 4.4x on 2026; (c) the gate's own share (7%) rests on 279 sampled rows; (d) restricting to the gate caps recall at 304/552 = 55%. Choosing 5% over 1% is not visibly driven by 2026, but it is also not the best on 2025: the 1% gate had higher 2025 precision (Opus 80 / 204).

checks.claim: A checker needs a positive likelihood ratio of about 31-43; achieved: checker v1 4.5, v2 4.0, Opus second look 1.08
checks.detail: Measured: from 154 / 6,665, keeping 60 at P50 needs sensitivity 0.390 and specificity 0.991, LR 43.3. From zs_and_rag 80 / 2,516: 0.75 / 0.976, LR 31.4. From the selector's 125 / 3,856: 0.48 / 0.984, LR 30.8. From the files results/rare_check/metrics_2026.json and _v2.json: v1 keeps 73 / 500.5, so sensitivity 0.584, specificity 0.870, LR 4.50. The Opus verdict keeps 94 / 2,690.6, so 0.752 / 0.302, LR 1.08. Caveats: the 'after check' false count includes fallback answers that may themselves be rare, so these are approximate LRs; and the specificity rests on few sampled reports.

checks.claim: Per-code false counts swing between years (Opus zs: Prophylactic removal 1,898 [10] -> 497 [3]; Failure to Reset 1,328 [7] -> 2,463 [15]; Battery High Impedance 570 [3] -> 1,643 [10]) and this drift is a cause of bad corrected counts
checks.detail: Numbers measured and matched: 1,898.1 [10] -> 497.1 [3], 1,327.6 [7] -> 2,463.4 [15], 570.5 [3] -> 1,643.2 [10]. Calling this 'drift' is not supported. With equal-size draws, an exact conditional binomial test gives two-sided p of about 0.09, 0.13 and 0.09, which I computed by hand: none of the three swings exceeds what sampling noise alone gives. The conclusion that per-code correction fails still holds, but the reason is sampling coarseness, not shown year-to-year change. I did not rerun the median-error table (5.5 vs 5.1 and so on) or the detection z-values (s4/s5).

checks.claim: Cost figures (GPU-hours, Opus tokens) and the gated-census cost of 8-13 GPU-hours
checks.detail: Not rechecked. I skipped s3_cost. The '1.4k-2.8k LLM calls' certification number is arithmetic I confirmed (2.996 / (100 / 46,149) = 1,382). It is a within-gate random sample, not the 'exact census' of all ~46k gated reports that the same sentence promises. Those are two different designs, with costs that differ by about 30x.

corrections: The 'drift between years' behind the per-code swings is not shown: the three cited swings (10->3, 7->15, 3->10 sampled) are each within binomial sampling noise (two-sided p of about 0.09-0.13). Call it sampling coarseness.
The gated false count for Opus (1,526 a year) rests on 9 sampled reports (rough 95% range of about 670-2,800). The 'cuts false about 4x' figure is a point estimate, and the same gate cut 11x on 2025.

'Exact census of about 46k reports' and 'testable for about 1.4k-2.8k LLM calls' are two different designs: the census needs the LLM on all ~46k gated reports; 1,382 calls is a random subsample inside the gate, and it certifies <=100 only if zero false are seen.
'40 to 100 times too loose' is loose: against P50 at each coder's own recall the factor is about 43x (Opus) and about 112x (Qwen); across the P50 R10-R50 range it is 24-266x.
The gate restricts recall to at most 304/552 (55%). Encoder npz argmax disagrees with the stored encoder answer on about 0.4-0.6% of balanced rows, a minor inconsistency in the gate input.
check.net: Every main measured number reproduces with my own tally. That includes the loader structure: no key overlap between the balanced and natural parts, weights adding up to 661,160, 552 rare reports, and a correct 1-5 rare cut. It also includes the base-rate map, each coder's place on it, the 498-a-year blind spot of the 3,974-report draw, the checker LR arithmetic and the 2025-set encoder gate (123 / 1,526 [9] for Opus). The central conclusion follows from the numbers: at 0.083% prevalence, zero-shot LLMs are tens to hundreds of times too loose, the strict rules have 4-6% recall, and the current uniform draw cannot measure any P50 rule. The weaker parts are the following. The 'drift' explanation for bad per-code counts is unsupported, since sampling noise alone covers the swings. The gate's benefit on 2026 rests on 9-18 sampled false reports and was much smaller than on 2025. The 'exact census' and '1.4k-2.8k calls' framings describe different designs. I did not recheck the cost figures, the corrected-count error table or the detection z-values.

prep.composition: There are 183 items after removing duplicates (measured). Per group: G1 43, G2 40, G3 40, G4 30, G5 40, G6 20. 26 items belong to more than one group: G1+G3 12, G1+G2 6, G2+G3 4, G1+G2+G3 4. There are 172 distinct templates (Jaccard of 0.8 or more on token sets after digit and whitespace normalisation, single linkage; a template also joins items from the same report). 8 templates hold more than one item, and the largest holds 4. The filed code is on side A in 86 items and on side B in 97. No text was longer than 3,000 characters, so none was cut; lengths run from 51 to 2,471 characters. Every blind line has only the fields id, text, A and B. The seed is 20261111.
prep.notes:
All figures here were measured by build_audit.py unless marked otherwise.

The loader passed the sanity check. The encoder in 2026 gives 32.0 right and 166.0 false rare answers a year (1 false in the sample), with uniform-draw accuracy 0.6365. The zero-shot coder names a rare code on 88 of the 3,974 frequent-code reports in the uniform draw for Qwen, 87 for Gemma and 40 for Opus, and all of them are false. All of this matches the known values.

How the groups were built:
- **G1:** I took all 4,000 rows of the uniform draw (U). There were 58 cases of a coder and report where Opus zs or rag names a rare code that is not the filed one. They became 43 items because zs and rag often named the same code; the key lists each item's sources. 2 items are rag-only.
- **G2 and G3:** Qwen had 89 candidates covering 19 distinct codes, and Gemma had 87 covering 15. Qwen has 89 here against 88 above because U includes one row whose filed code is not frequent. I spread each 40 across the named codes in proportion, using largest remainder, then picked at random within each code.
- **G4:** I treated the rare census as the natural-sample rare 1-5 stratum, which has 80 candidates, plus the rare-code reports in the 2026 balanced test, which have 50. Both carry weight 1 and are part of the 552. From these 130 I drew 30: 22 from the natural sample and 8 from the balanced test. This pooling was my choice. The balanced keys also use the 2026 pool. In one G4 item the encoder's answer is itself another rare code.
- **G5 and G6:** G5 drew from 2,138 candidates and G6 from 327.

Odd points:
1. **Zero weight.** One G6 item (report 24073392, filed code with 9 training reports) has a whole-year weight of 0.0. It is in the uniform draw but not in the 6-20 stratum, and natural_weights gives uniform rows weight only when the filed code has 21 or more training reports. Every other item weighs 164.025 (uniform) or 1.0 (G4).
2. **Repeated reports.** Four reports appear in two items with different pairs, so readers will see the same text twice: 24334255, 50321627, 50450719 and 25436160. Two of them have different rare codes from Opus and from Qwen or Gemma. One is in G3 and G5.
3. **Templates.** Template 2 is the known pacemaker battery template: filed as Premature Discharge of Battery against Battery Problem: High Impedance, with 3 items in G1, G2 and G3. Template 152 has 4 near-identical texts across G5 and G6 whose filed codes differ: 2 are filed as Incorrect/Imprecise Readings and 2 as High Readings.
4. **Attractor codes.** The most frequent other codes in G1 are Failure to Reset (15), Battery Problem: High Impedance (10), Prophylactic removal due to corrective action (4) and Application Program Problem: Medication Error (3).
5. **Lowercased texts.** Texts are the lowercased versions from maude_data.canonical, which is what the coders saw, not the original upper-case text.
6. **Pool scan.** I scanned the 2026 pool once and cached 9,741 keys in the scratch file cache_pool2026.pkl. load_coders was patched to read from that cache.

The key file also holds, for each item: which coders named the other code and which named the filed code, the training count of each code, the sample part, and the text length.

Nothing was written to the repository. No GPU or API was used. I made no judgement of any item.

reads.impressions:
All 183 items are judged, in order, and the file passes a format check (ids 1 to 183, valid JSON on every line). Choices: A 81, B 75, both 11, neither 9, unclear 7.

Recurring report templates. Most pairs were easy because the text names the problem outright:
- **Tandem pump "malfunction code ... could not be reset":** about 25 items. Failure to Reset was always against Pumping Stopped, and Failure to Reset matches the wording, so I picked it. The "speaker" alarm variants went to Defective Alarm when that code was offered.
- **Boston Scientific "code 1003, voltage too low ... potential high impedance within the battery":** about 12 items. Battery High Impedance (stated outright) was against Premature Discharge, and I picked High Impedance.
- **Joint revision reports saying "subsidence":** Implant subsidence was against Migration, and I picked subsidence.
- **Philips vulnerability scans:** Computer System Security was against an unrelated code such as Radiation Output Failure.
- **BD Pyxis dispensing faults:** Medication Error was against Labelling or Electrical.
- **Other repeating groups:**
  - Abbott CGM high or low readings (the specific leaf won)
  - Olympus reprocessing and contamination
  - lap-sponge or gauze extra-count packs (Extra Components)
  - iLet "usage problem / improper procedure" (the specific leaf won)
  - Medtronic "updated summary" stubs with no content (marked unclear)

Hard pairs:
1. **Parent code against its own child** when the text is vague. Examples: "pacing issue" against Pacing Inadequately, "inappropriate pacing", LV dysfunction from RV pacing, "low heart rates", capsular contracture against Rejection, and Medication Error against the generic Application Program code.
2. **Near-synonym siblings**:
   - Detachment against Decoupling (infusion sets falling off, a syringe nozzle detached, a device off the back plate)
   - Puncture/Hole against Split/Torn ("hole that appeared shredded")
   - Failure to Fire against Failure to Form Staple
   - Blockage against Filtration ("clogged/defective filter")
   - Crystallization coded as Precipitate against Failure to Clean
3. **Clinical reports that explicitly say the device was not at fault**: Impella cases, LVAD right heart failure, DKA blamed on illness, sepsis with a drape. In these, "Prophylactic removal due to corrective action" was often one candidate and rarely fit, so I chose neither or the generic Patient Device Interaction code.
4. **Removals or revisions with an unknown reason**, and content-free updates, which I marked unclear.

The "Prophylactic removal due to corrective action" code appeared often as a candidate and fit only a few items: recalled pods, foam replaced preventatively, and arguably an explant at the patient's request.

My literal flags are strict: a code counts as literal only when its wording, such as "reset", "subsidence", "high impedance" or "bent", appears in the text.

I judged all 183 items, starting from the last and working back to item 1. Each item has one line in the file, with no duplicates or gaps.

Recurring report templates:
(1) Tandem insulin pump "malfunction code/alarm ... could not be reset" (about 20 items). Each pairs Failure to Reset with Pumping Stopped. The text literally says "could not be reset" but almost never says delivery stopped. I gave these a slight edge to the Failure to Reset code (strength 1). When an undertravel or motor stall was named I called it "both". When the alarm was described as a speaker problem and the reset worked, I preferred Defective Alarm.
(2) Boston Scientific pacemaker "code 1003, voltage too low ... potential high impedance within the battery" (about 13 items). Each pairs High Impedance with Premature Discharge. I consistently picked High Impedance (strength 2) because it is literal.
(3) Philips "vulnerability scan/report" items. One of the pair was Computer System Security Problem and the other an unrelated code such as Radiation Output Failure or Unable to Obtain Readings, so these were easy.
(4) BD Pyxis items ("not crossing over", critical override, wrong drawer opening). I usually preferred the Medication Error software code over the Labelling, Installation or Electrical codes. The password/biometric login item fit neither code well.
(5) Abbott sensor discrepancies, scored with the Parkes error grid. The specific High/Low Readings code beat the generic Incorrect Readings parent.
(6) Joint revision for implant subsidence. Implant subsidence beat Migration almost every time.
(7) iLet use-error template. I picked the parent or the child code (Improper Procedure) depending on whether the text named an improper procedure.
(8) Impella and LVAD narratives saying "device functioned as intended", which were weak for both codes.

Hard pairs:
- Parent versus child code where the text supports only the parent level: pacing issue, charging, reprocessing, Break versus Fracture.
- Decoupling versus Detachment versus Premature Separation for infusion sets coming off.
- Subsidence versus Dislodged when both happen.
- Capsular contracture: generic interaction versus Rejection.
- Near-empty texts ("updated summary", "no product return is required", "reason for revision unknown"), which I marked unclear.
- Literature reports and "not device related" narratives, which I marked neither.

Prophylactic removal due to corrective action appeared often, apparently as the automatic coder's fallback. It rarely fit, except for recall or revision-to-improve-fit cases.

Most "both" and strength-1 choices fall in the pump-reset and parent/child families.

I judged all 183 items in the order asked: 92 to 183 first, then 1 to 91. The output file has 183 lines with one entry for each id and none missing.

A few report templates make up much of the set, and each comes with the same two codes over and over:
(1) Tandem pump reports that say "malfunction code / could not be reset / replacement pump". The pair is always Failure to Reset vs Pumping Stopped. I picked Failure to Reset each time, because the text says it in so many words and never says delivery stopped. Where the text also says "undertravel stall" (172, 176) I called it both.
(2) Boston Scientific pacemaker "code 1003 ... potential high impedance within the battery". The pair is High Impedance vs Premature Discharge. High Impedance is plainly right every time.
(3) Philips vulnerability-scan complaints. The pair is Computer System Security vs a code that has nothing to do with the report (Radiation Output, Wireless, Unable to Obtain Readings, Self-Test). Easy.
(4) BD Pyxis reports: "not crossing over", critical override, wrong drawer opening, login problems. These are hard. The Medication Error software code fits only loosely, and the other code (Labelling, Installation, Electrical) usually fits even worse.
(5) Abbott CGM "erroneous results, Parkes C zone". The pair is the generic Incorrect Readings vs High or Low Readings. I chose the specific direction by comparing the sensor value with the meter value.
(6) iLet use-error reports. The pair is Use of Device vs Improper or Incorrect Procedure. The two are nearly interchangeable, so my choices here are weak.
(7) Joint revision reports that mention subsidence. The pair is Implant subsidence vs Migration, and subsidence is plainly right.
(8) Reprocessing reports from Olympus scopes (crystallization, foreign material, failed disinfection cycle, cultures). Several close parent/child or sibling pairs.
(9) Counts of surgical packs (11 vs 10 sponges). Extra Components is clearly right.

Two kinds of pairs were hard:
- A parent code against its own child. Here I took the child only when the text supports its specific detail.
- Reports that say almost nothing or describe no device problem: "updated summary: will not be returned", revisions for an unknown reason, LVAD right heart failure, Impella cases where the device "functioned as intended", and literature summaries. Here one or both codes is often "Prophylactic removal due to corrective action" or a generic Patient Device Interaction code. I marked these neither or unclear.

Items 80 and 85 have identical text but different code pairs. Items 4 and 115, and 47 and 155, are also repeated texts with different pairs.

Overall, the code in a pair that echoes the report's wording usually looked better, and the pairs where one code was clearly unrelated came mostly from the vulnerability, Pyxis and "no apparent adverse event" filler templates.

score.headline: All three readers judged all 183 items, and they agreed strongly: Fleiss kappa 0.85, with 157 of 183 items unanimous. On the Opus false rare answers (G1, 43 items covering nearly every Opus false rare answer in the 2026 uniform draw), the reader majority preferred Opus's rare code on 36 of 43 (0.84) and the filed code on only 1. That is the same as how often the readers side with Opus on ordinary frequent-code disagreements (G5: 35 of 40, 0.88; difference -0.04, CI -0.19 to +0.11). So the Opus-family readers simply side with Opus about 85% of the time, whether or not the code is rare, and this does not show the filed codes are wrong. On the Qwen and Gemma false rare answers, readers preferred the LLM code on only 18 of 40 and 17 of 40, and the filed code on 10 of 40 each. That is clearly below the G5 baseline (differences -0.42 and -0.45; CIs exclude zero). Where Opus did not name the same code, it drops to 13 of 50 for the LLM code against 18 of 50 for the filed code. Most of what looks like Opus error comes from two manufacturer templates: Tandem 'could not be reset', filed as Pumping Stopped, and Boston Scientific 'high impedance within the battery', filed as Premature Discharge. These make up 25 of the 43 G1 items. In both, the text states the rare code's wording outright, but the manufacturer always files a different, frequent code. So much of the 'false rare answer' problem is a mismatch between what the text literally says and the filing convention, not a misreading. The exception is the attractor 'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action', which readers almost never endorse (4 of 31 items across G1-G3). Both controls (G4 rare census, G6) went to the filed code, which equals Opus's answer, on 28 of 30 and 18 of 20, as expected; by design they cannot separate good reading from a bias toward the LLM.

findings.claim: Coverage is complete and agreement between readers is high.
findings.evidence: All 183 items were judged by all 3 readers (183 judged by 3, 0 by 2, 0 by 1); no ids missing or extra. Pairwise exact agreement on 5 categories (other/filed/both/neither/unclear), with Cohen kappa: r1-r2 0.918 (0.869), r1-r3 0.885 (0.818), r2-r3 0.913 (0.862). Fleiss kappa 0.850 on 5 categories and 0.846 on 3 (other/filed/tie). 157 of 183 items unanimous; no item without a 2-of-3 majority.

findings.claim: G1 (Opus false rare answers): the majority prefers the Opus code on 84% of items, which is the same rate as on ordinary disagreements (G5).
findings.evidence: G1 n=43 (40 templates): other 36, both 3, neither 2, unclear 1, filed 1. Share other 0.84 (template cluster bootstrap CI 0.71-0.94), filed 0.02 (0-0.07). One vote per template 0.82; one vote per code pair (19 families) 0.76; weighted by whole year (all weights 164.025) 0.84. G5 n=40: other 35, filed 3, both 2 (0.88, CI 0.77-0.97). G1 minus G5 = -0.04 (CI -0.19 to +0.11 by template clusters; -0.25 to +0.11 clustered by code pair). Opus zs items: 35 of 40 other; Opus rag items: 16 of 18 other.

findings.claim: G2 and G3 (Qwen and Gemma false rare answers): readers side with the LLM much less often than on the G5 baseline. A quarter of the items clearly favour the filed code, and about a quarter favour neither or are unclear.
findings.evidence: G2 Qwen n=40: other 18 (0.45, CI 0.30-0.60), filed 10 (0.25, 0.12-0.40), both 3, neither 5, unclear 4. G3 Gemma n=40: other 17 (0.42, 0.26-0.60), filed 10 (0.25, 0.12-0.39), both 1, neither 7, unclear 5. Difference from G5: G2 -0.42 (CI -0.60 to -0.23), G3 -0.45 (-0.64 to -0.25); clustered by code pair -0.65 to -0.21 and -0.72 to -0.22. When Opus also named the same rare code: G2 8 of 10 other, G3 13 of 16 other. When Opus did not: G2 10 of 30 other, 10 filed; G3 4 of 24 other, 10 filed.

findings.claim: Two manufacturer templates account for most of the G1 endorsements: the text literally names the rare code, but the filing convention uses a frequent sibling code.
findings.evidence: G1 per attractor: Failure to Reset vs filed Pumping Stopped, 15 items: other 13, both 2. Battery Problem: High Impedance vs filed Premature Discharge of Battery, 10 items: other 10. The same two families in G2 (5+3 items) and G3 (7+5) are all other or both. Without these two families: G1 13 of 18 other; G2 10 of 32 other vs 10 filed; G3 6 of 28 other vs 10 filed.

findings.claim: The attractor 'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action' is a genuine false answer: readers almost never endorse it.
findings.evidence: Majority on items where this was the LLM code: G1 4 items (other 1, neither 2, unclear 1); G2 9 items (other 2, filed 1, neither 2, unclear 4); G3 18 items (other 1, filed 7, neither 6, unclear 4). Pacing Inadequately (a child code against its filed parent Pacing Problem): G2 other 1 of 5 vs filed 4; G3 filed 1, unclear 1.

findings.claim: Literal marks: on false rare answers, the text often names the LLM's code word for word and seldom names the filed code. When it does name the LLM's code, readers almost always side with the LLM.
findings.evidence: Items where at least 2 of 3 readers mark the LLM code literal and the filed code not literal: G1 27 of 43, G2 8 of 40, G3 12 of 40, G5 12 of 40. The reverse (filed literal only): G1 2, G2 3, G3 4, G5 2. Among items with the LLM code literal only, the majority is other in 44 of 47 (G1 25 other + 2 both; G2 8 of 8; G3 11 + 1 both). On items without that pattern: G1 11 of 16 other; G2 10 of 32; G3 6 of 28. Reader-level share of LLM-literal-only: G1 0.63, G2 0.22, G3 0.30. Readers' literal flags are strict (wording must appear in the text).

findings.claim: Yearly picture for Opus zero-shot (about 6,665 false rare answers a year; 40 sampled in the uniform draw): about 5,800 a year are judged a better fit than the filed code, about 300 equal, about 170 worse, and about 330 neither.
findings.evidence: Opus zs items (n=40): other 0.88 [0.76-0.97] -> ~5,832/yr [5,044-6,494] (35 of 40 sampled); both 0.05 -> ~333 [0-877] (2); filed 0.03 -> ~167 [0-526] (1); neither 0.05 -> ~333 [0-854] (2); unclear 0. The brackets cover only the share's uncertainty. The yearly total rests on 40 sampled reports itself; a Poisson 95% range of roughly 29-55 sampled (my calculation, not computed in the script) means roughly ±30% more. About 2,500 a year (15 of 40) are the Tandem reset template and about 1,600 (10) the battery template, so these two conventions make up most of the total.
findings.reproduce: score.py YEARLY section; the Poisson range and template-per-year figures are arithmetic (inferred)

findings.claim: Yearly picture for Qwen and Gemma (zero-shot, 40 items read out of 88 and 87 sampled): fewer than half are judged better than the filed code; about a quarter are worse and about a quarter neither or unclear.
findings.evidence: Qwen (~14,693/yr): other 0.45 [0.30-0.60] -> ~6,600/yr [4,400-8,800]; both 0.07 -> ~1,100; filed 0.25 [0.12-0.40] -> ~3,700 [1,800-5,900]; neither 0.12 -> ~1,800; unclear 0.10 -> ~1,500. Gemma (~14,476/yr): other 0.42 [0.26-0.60] -> ~6,150 [3,800-8,600]; both 0.03 -> ~360; filed 0.25 [0.12-0.39] -> ~3,600 [1,800-5,700]; neither 0.17 -> ~2,500; unclear 0.12 -> ~1,800. Sampled equivalents: about 40 of 88 and 37 of 87 other; about 22 of 88 and 22 of 87 filed. Template cluster bootstrap; the uncertainty in the yearly total is not included.

findings.claim: Controls: readers pick the filed code (which equals Opus's answer) over the encoder's answer in G4 and G6, as both an LLM-biased reader and a good reader would.
findings.evidence: G4 (rare census, filed is the rare code, other is the encoder's answer, Opus zs names the filed code in 30 of 30): filed 28, both 2, other 0; mean strength 2.53 (highest of any group); filed literal only 15 of 30. G6 (frequent, encoder wrong, Opus zs names the filed code in 20 of 20): filed 18, other 2. By design these cannot separate reading skill from a pull toward the LLM's answer.

findings.claim: Readers' confidence is lower on the Qwen and Gemma rare items than on the controls.
findings.evidence: Mean strength (1-3) over readers: G1 1.89, G2 1.69, G3 1.77, G4 2.53, G5 1.90, G6 2.00.

findings.claim: Most Opus false rare answers look like a mismatch between the text and the filing convention, not misreading. The real misreads are the generic attractors (Prophylactic removal, child-for-parent pacing codes), which Qwen and Gemma produce much more often than Opus.
findings.evidence: The template families, literal marks and attractor tables above. Prophylactic removal appears in 4 G1 items vs 9 G2 and 18 G3. 25 of 43 G1 items are the two convention templates.

findings.claim: Eight short examples (text cut to its key words; the code paths are shortened). Readers clearly prefer the LLM code: (#3, Opus+Qwen) 'pump displayed malfunction code and could not be reset ... no adverse impact', LLM Failure to Reset vs filed Pumping Stopped, 3/3 for the LLM. (#43, Qwen) 'infusion set tubing pulled off partly accidentally by getting caught on some object', LLM Decoupling vs filed Use of Incorrect Control/Treatment Settings, 3/3 for the LLM. Readers clearly prefer the filed code: (#147, Opus) 'bd pyxis medflex ... unable to issue oxycodone 5 mg tablets ... medication did not appear in the patient order list', LLM Application Program Problem: Medication Error vs filed Use of Device Problem, 3/3 for the filed code. (#19, Gemma) 'extensions were causing the impedances and not the ipg', LLM Prophylactic removal vs filed Impedance Problem, 3/3 for the filed code. (#36, Qwen) 'right atrial lead exhibited inappropriate pacing at times', LLM Pacing Inadequately vs filed Pacing Problem, 3/3 for the filed code. Both fit: (#75, Qwen) 'infusion set was leaking due to tubing detachment', LLM Decoupling vs filed Fluid/Blood Leak, 3/3 both. Unclear or neither: (#138, Gemma) 'brady lead ... due to an unknown product performance anomaly. a new lead ... was implanted', LLM Pacing Inadequately vs filed Material Integrity Problem, 3/3 unclear. (#21, Gemma) Impella CP narrative, urine discoloration 'not suspected to be related', LLM Prophylactic removal vs filed Patient Device Interaction Problem, 2/3 neither and 1/3 filed.
findings.evidence: Item ids are blind ids; votes and texts are printed in extra_out.txt.

caveats: The readers are Opus agents, the same model family as one of the coders. Their 84-88% siding with Opus (G1, G5) is partly a shared reading habit, so it does not show that the filed code is wrong. The Qwen and Gemma items are the cleaner test, and even there agreement is higher when Opus also named the code (21 of 26 vs 14 of 54 other).

No human has read any of these items. The filed MAUDE code is the manufacturer's choice and follows its own conventions, so 'reader prefers the LLM code' means the text reads that way, not that the code is clinically or regulatorily right.

G5's high siding with Opus (35 of 40) means the readers favour the LLM even on ordinary frequent-code disagreements, so G5 is a baseline for reader bias, not a measure of filed-code accuracy. G1 matching G5 is consistent both with 'Opus rare answers are as good as its ordinary disagreements' and with 'readers simply follow Opus'.

The template clustering (Jaccard >= 0.8) splits the Tandem reset and Boston Scientific battery texts into many templates, so one vote per template barely changes anything. One vote per code pair (19 G1 families) gives 0.76 other, and that is probably the fairer count.

The yearly figures multiply a share by a yearly total that rests on 40, 88 or 87 sampled reports (1 sampled report is about 164 reports a year); the brackets show only the share's bootstrap uncertainty. Only 40 of 88 Qwen and 40 of 87 Gemma candidates were read.

Four reports appear in two items each (e.g. #15 and #12 share text: readers endorsed Opus's Failure to Disinfect but rejected Qwen/Gemma's Problem with Sterilization on the same report), so items are not fully independent.
I used no 2026-tuned choices; this is scoring only. Nothing was written to the repo; no GPU or API was used.
leads: Treat the two convention templates (Tandem 'could not be reset' -> Pumping Stopped; Boston Scientific code 1003 'high impedance' -> Premature Discharge) as a label-mapping problem: learn manufacturer and template -> filed-code conventions from 2024/2025 (for example, a nearest-neighbour template match that overrides an LLM rare answer when 2024 near-duplicates are all filed as one frequent code). CPU only. Check it on 2025 first; this alone would remove about 25 of the 40 sampled Opus false rare answers.

Put a filter on generic attractor codes such as Prophylactic removal due to corrective action, and on child-for-parent pacing codes: require the LLM's rare answer to be supported by the text (a literal cue or retrieval support) before accepting it. Set the rule on 2024/2025. CPU only.

Reframe the target: report 'text-supported rare finding' (the text names a rare problem) separately from 'filed code'. The readers suggest a large part of the false rare answers are text-correct but convention-wrong, so a review queue for rare findings may be the more useful product than matching the filed code.
Get a small human read (a domain expert, 30-50 items from G2/G3 plus the two convention templates) to break the Opus-reader confound. Needs a human.

Re-run the blind reading with a non-Opus reader (local Qwen or Gemma as judge, each judging the other's items) to measure how much of the G1/G5 siding is family bias. Needs the GPU, so only with the user's go-ahead.
surprises: Opus's false rare answers are endorsed at the same rate as its ordinary frequent-code disagreements (0.84 vs 0.88), and only 1 of 43 G1 items has a filed-code majority.

On the very same report (colonoscope 'unable to complete the disinfection cycle'), readers endorsed Opus's Failure to Disinfect 3/3 but rejected Qwen/Gemma's Problem with Sterilization 3/3: the choice of rare sibling matters, not only rarity.
Gemma's most common false rare answer is Prophylactic removal due to corrective action (18 of 40 items), and readers endorse it on only 1.
Readers were most confident on G4 (rare filed code vs encoder, mean strength 2.53, 28 of 30 filed). When the rare code is right, the text tends to say so clearly.

critic.answer_so_far: Yes, the binding problem is that zero-shot LLMs put rare codes on ordinary reports. The cause is not a special bias toward rare codes. The LLMs have almost no frequency prior across the tail: answer-count slope on training share is -0.07 to 0.11 below 100 training reports, against 0.65 for the filed codes. At a prevalence of 1 in 1,198 this flat prior gives false-alarm rates of 1 in 45 to 1 in 100 ordinary reports and rare-code precision of 0.9-2.3%. A 50%-precision rule needs a rate 40-266 times lower, so per-report labelling of rare codes at natural proportions is dead for every coder tried. No zero-shot model or prompt variant comes close, and the rules strict enough to get there reach only 4-5% recall. The false answers are not random noise. They pile onto a few attractor codes, and those codes are the same across the three LLMs and repeat from 2025 to 2026. For Opus, about 25 of 40 sampled false answers come from two manufacturer templates whose text literally names the rare code ('could not be reset', 'high impedance within the battery') while the manufacturer always files a frequent sibling. Blinded Opus readers back the LLM there, but they back Opus just as often on ordinary disagreements (0.84 vs 0.88), so this is a text-versus-convention mismatch, not proof that the filed code is wrong. Qwen and Gemma make real misreads more often, above all 'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action', which readers almost never endorse (4 of 31 items). That code is the only listed child of a branch whose 'no problem' parent was removed when the label list was built. A second limit holds regardless of false alarms: only 219 of the 552 rare reports have any coder right, and even a perfect chooser over richer candidate lists reaches only 243-297. The misses sit in a few codes that are new or fast-growing 2026 filing habits. The only strong unused veto signal is the encoder's rank for the code the LLM proposed (unweighted AUC 0.80-0.88). Every gain it gives over the known rules is within 0-3 sampled reports, and the 3,974-report uniform draw cannot check any useful precision target: zero sampled false still allows about 500 a year. The better problems are four. (a) A ranked review queue gated by encoder rare-probability or encoder rank, measured by a census inside the gate. (b) Fixing the label list: restore the removed 'no problem' codes and hidden parents, and add an abstain option. (c) A screen that flags reports whose text names a rare finding the filed code does not carry. (d) Group-level counting or new-habit detection instead of per-report rare labels.
contradictions: Templates: overnaming says false-rare reports cluster no more than random reports (whole-text TF-IDF at cos>=0.8). Convention and the audit say two template families make up 25 of the 40 Opus false answers (25 of 43 G1 items). Both hold: the templates share a key phrase but differ in the rest of the text. Phrase-level templates dominate Opus's errors; Qwen and Gemma errors (Prophylactic removal) are not template-driven.

Using the encoder as a veto: convention's check shows that 'encoder names a frequent code' kills 129 of Opus's 154 right rare answers. History and signals show that the encoder's rank for the proposed code separates right from false well (false answers are in the encoder's top 10 for 2-4%, right answers for 50-65%). Encoder top-1 disagreement is useless as a veto; the encoder's rank for the proposed code is the useful signal.

Overnaming's headline 'no special bias toward rare codes' against its own 19-44x over-naming. Per code, the false rate is ordinary only by the band mean, which the attractor codes drive. By the median, rare codes are named falsely less often (0 vs 5e-4). The flat prior is itself the bias.

Ceiling says the misses are mostly a label problem and only a small coder problem. The check says this is not shown: it rests on one reader's 40 items, and agreement between three LLMs that share one prompt is not independent support. The audit's G4 readers side strongly with the filed rare code when it is right (28 of 30), but G4 contains only rows where Opus already named that code.

Signals says the 2025-frozen thresholds work only in hindsight. The check finds that a stricter 2025 rule lands on the known 2026 frontier. The honest reading: no measurable gain and no measurable loss.

Literature says every published correction reduces to Saerens, which was already tried. The check notes that confusion-matrix and BBSE estimators on hard answers, and Monte-Carlo generative calibration, are different methods that need no logprobs.

Drift from 2025 to 2026: arithmetic attributes per-code swings in false counts to drift, but they are within binomial noise (p about 0.09-0.13). Convention splits the encoder's accuracy fall into one quarter composition and three quarters within-bin; finer bins give about one third composition.

Precision bound: overnaming used only the 291-report census (70-150x gap). With all 552 rare reports the gap is 40-105x. Literature says the encoder meets the target, but it sits at 166 false against 165.6 allowed, from 1 sampled report, so that is not established.
History's reweighted Opus 2025 count (4,072 false) against the natural sample (6,698). 'Reasoning helps' rests on the same 31 sampled false items under both settings.
Ceiling's 'top 3 codes by size hold 129 misses' is really sorted by miss count; by size it is 99.
gaps: Nobody tested causally whether restoring the removed 'no problem' codes (A24-A27), the hidden parents (Battery Problem, Connection Problem) or an abstain option removes the attractors. That they come from the list is a structural inference only.
No human, and no reader outside the Opus family, has judged any item. The audit's 84-88% siding with Opus is confounded with a shared reading habit.
Nobody checked the alphabetical-position or primacy effect of the 424-label list on false rare answers, although it can be tested on stored outputs.
Nobody measured how many false rare answers a census inside a gate would show; every strict rule's false count rests on 0-4 sampled reports (each about 164 a year).
Nobody computed what the false side looks like on the 51,153 reports (7.2%) of 2026 whose codes are hidden or unlisted; the deployed false load is probably larger.
No manufacturer or product-code data exist for 2025 and 2026, so filing conventions per manufacturer cannot be learned or tested.
Nobody checked whether a phrase-level convention map (e.g. 'could not be reset' -> Pumping Stopped) would also kill right rare answers on the census.
Nobody tested whether the 333 always-missed reports could be reached by retraining the encoder with 2025 data, or whether they are learnable conventions at all.
Group-level quantification (BBSE over all rare codes pooled) was not run; only per-code adjusted counting was, and it failed.
The concentration of the raw-stream 'copy earlier identical report' result (65% coverage at 96.5%) in a few huge templates was not measured.
Nobody has counted SDR's natural proportions; the SDR figures are reweighted estimates only.

hypotheses.statement: Zero-shot LLMs answer with a near-flat prior over the tail, so at 0.083% prevalence their rare-code precision is capped at about 1-2%. No zero-shot model or prompt variant tried escapes this; per-report rare labelling at natural proportions with these coders is dead.
hypotheses.support: Poisson slope -0.07 to 0.11 below 100 training reports, rechecked. False-alarm rate 1 in 45 to 1 in 100 ordinary reports, rechecked. 50% precision needs 40-266x lower. All 10 model variants make thousands of false answers a year. The strict rules have recall of 4-5%.

hypotheses.statement: False rare answers are text-driven and concentrate on a few attractor codes that persist across models and years.
hypotheses.support: Top 5 codes carry 69-85% of false answers. Overlap between pairs of LLMs is 22-35x chance, nearly always on the same code. The 2025-2026 Spearman is 0.52-0.78, and 4 of the top 5 codes repeat. Rechecked except the persistence figures.

hypotheses.statement: For Opus, most 'false' rare answers are literal readings of a few manufacturer templates whose filing convention uses a frequent sibling. They are false against the key, but the text supports them.
hypotheses.support: Two families make up 25 of 40 sampled Opus false answers (rechecked). Blinded readers back the LLM 25 of 25 on them, and the LLM wording is marked literal on 27 of 43 G1 items. The readers are Opus-family; G1 matches the G5 baseline, so the support is confounded. The yearly counts rest on two clustered families.

hypotheses.statement: The construction of the closed label list creates some attractors: the orphan child A2501 'Prophylactic removal' under a removed 'no problem' parent, 'Battery Problem: High Impedance' with its parent hidden, and no abstain option. Qwen and Gemma's top false code is a genuine misread created by the list.
hypotheses.support: Structure verified: A2501 kept while A24-A27 were removed, and 47 codes hidden including Battery Problem (5,946 reports in 2026). Readers endorse Prophylactic removal on 4 of 31 items. Opus tried unlisted answers such as 'Insufficient Information'. No run with these labels restored exists.

hypotheses.statement: Recall is capped independently of false alarms: about 60% of 2026 rare reports are unreachable for every coder. The misses sit in a few new or growing filing habits, and better candidate lists cannot fix them.
hypotheses.support: 219 of 552 found by any of the 7 answers; a perfect chooser reaches 243-297; 2025 TF-IDF neighbours hold the filed code for 72. Misses concentrate in Medication Error, Power Conditioning and Security codes. Rechecked except the 2025 kNN result.

hypotheses.statement: Those misses are mostly label or convention problems rather than coder errors.
hypotheses.support: One reader's 40 items (23 'coder answer as good', 6 'label wrong'). Three LLMs agree on another code, but they share one prompt. Lenient scoring raises recall to 357. Not shown.

hypotheses.statement: The encoder's rank or log-probability for the code the LLM proposed is the only strong signal for vetting LLM rare answers. LLM agreement, word overlap and multi-feature models add nothing, and any gain over the known rules is not measurable with the current sample.
hypotheses.support: AUC 0.80-0.88 unweighted, rechecked. All three LLMs agreeing is still 99 right / 2,977 false (18 sampled). The combined model is no better. Frozen points move by 0-3 sampled reports.

hypotheses.statement: The current evaluation design cannot verify any rule with precision of 50% or more; only a census inside a gate can.
hypotheses.support: Zero sampled false in 3,974 reports still allows about 500 a year, more than the whole 50%-precision budget up to 50% recall. The encoder gate keeps 304 of 552 rare reports while flagging 7% of reports. Arithmetic rechecked.

hypotheses.statement: Stronger models or reasoning solve the problem.
hypotheses.support: Opus with high-effort reasoning shows 31 sampled false, the same as plain Opus; the best variants still make about 3,000-6,700 false a year.

next_tests.what: Blinded label-list test with Opus agents acting as the coder. Code a small set (the 43 G1 items plus 80 G2/G3 items, the 30 G4 rare rights, and about 100 random frequent uniform reports) twice: once with the current 424-label prompt, and once with A24-A27 'no problem / insufficient information', the hidden parents (Battery Problem, Connection Problem) and an explicit 'answer the parent if the child is not stated' rule restored. Score attractor answers and rare rights kept.
next_tests.why: This is the only causal test of whether list construction creates the attractors (H4). If Prophylactic removal and child-for-parent answers vanish while G4 rights survive, the fix is cheap and frozen.
next_tests.expected_gain: Settles H4. Shows whether a large share of Qwen/Gemma-type misreads can be removed without new training.

next_tests.what: Break the reader confound: a human reader (or a domain expert) judges 30-50 blinded items from G2/G3 plus the two convention templates and some G5 items, using the existing blind file.
next_tests.why: Every 'text supports the LLM' claim (H3, H6) rests on Opus-family readers who back Opus at the same rate on ordinary disagreements.
next_tests.expected_gain: Tells whether the Opus 'false' rare answers measure filing convention or model error, which decides whether a text-vs-filed-code screen is a meaningful product.

next_tests.what: Review-queue evaluation on stored outputs. Rank all LLM rare proposals by the encoder's rank or log-probability for the proposed code (rule and k fixed on 2025nat and 2024val before opening 2026). Report rare reports found per review budget (0.1%, 0.5%, 1% of the year) for 2026, scored once.
next_tests.why: Turns the one strong signal into the reframed target. Recall at a budget is measurable on census rows with weight 1, unlike the precision of the false side.
next_tests.expected_gain: A frozen, honestly measurable headline for the reframed problem.

next_tests.what: List-position test: correlate per-code false-rare rate (pooled uniform, 2025+2026) with the code's alphabetical position in the prompt and with whether it is an only child or has a hidden parent.
next_tests.why: Cheap check of a primacy effect, and of the structural-orphan explanation, before any new LLM run.
next_tests.expected_gain: Rules a position explanation in or out; supports or weakens H4 without a run.

next_tests.what: Phrase-level convention veto: from 2024+2025 filings, learn short phrase -> filed-code maps (e.g. 'could not be reset' -> Pumping Stopped, 'code 1003' -> Premature Discharge). Veto an LLM rare answer when its report matches a phrase whose 2024-2025 filings are at least 90% one frequent code. Freeze on 2025 and count the rare rights it kills on the 2026 census.
next_tests.why: Targets the two templates behind most Opus false answers without the encoder top-1 veto, which kills 84% of rights.
next_tests.expected_gain: Could remove about 60% of Opus false answers. The census shows the cost exactly.

next_tests.what: Group-level quantification: estimate the total number of rare-code reports a year (all 46 codes pooled, and per IMDRF level-1 family) with BBSE / confusion-matrix correction calibrated on 2025nat, with intervals, checked 2024val->2025 and then 2025->2026.
next_tests.why: Per-code adjusted counts failed. Pooling may be within reach and fits the counting reframe; BBSE was never tried.
next_tests.expected_gain: Says whether counting replaces labelling at any useful grain, or is dead too.

next_tests.what: Gated census: run the encoder on all 2025 and 2026 reports, then Qwen or Gemma zero-shot and retrieval on every report whose encoder rare-mass is at least 0.00354 (about 7%, about 46-50k reports a year, 8-19 GPU-hours).
next_tests.why: The only way to measure false counts of strict rules exactly instead of from 0-4 sampled reports.
next_tests.expected_gain: Settles every claim now inside sampling noise (gates, k=3 rule, encoder log-probability vetoes).

next_tests.what: Fetch 2025/2026 MAUDE device files (manufacturer, product code). Test a 'rare code seen with this product code or manufacturer' screen and per-manufacturer filing conventions.
next_tests.why: Manufacturer habits appear to drive both false rare answers and the misses. On 2024 the product-code screen removed 83-92% of false answers but also about half of the rights.
next_tests.expected_gain: Possibly the strongest convention signal; needs the user's approval to download.

next_tests.what: Second reader for the ceiling investigation's 40 missed reports (missed_sample.txt), and an Opus-agent reader pass over a representative random 60 of the 333 misses.
next_tests.why: The 'label problem, not coder problem' reading of the ceiling rests on one reader and a sample spread round-robin over codes.
next_tests.expected_gain: Decides whether the recall ceiling should be attacked at all, or redefined at parent level.

next_tests.what: Retrain the encoder with 2025 added and score the 2026 misses (Medication Error, Decoupling, Implant subsidence vs the 2026-only habits).
next_tests.why: Tests whether the misses are learnable conventions that drift faster than yearly retraining.
next_tests.expected_gain: Measures how much of the 333 a time-updated coder reaches.

refuted_or_weak: Dead: per-report rare-code labelling at natural proportions with precision of 50% or more by any current coder or combination. The gap is 40-266x, and strict rules have recall of 5% or less.
Dead: per-code adjusted classify-and-count. The corrected counts are worse than the raw counts, and the intervals run to thousands of reports a code.
Dead: LLM agreement as a cleaner (all three agreeing: 99 right / 2,977 false, 18 sampled), and Opus's second look as a checker (likelihood ratio 1.08).
Dead: the encoder top-1 'family veto'. The encoder names a frequent code on 129 of Opus's 154 right rare answers.
Dead: lenient (parent, child or sibling) scoring as a fix for the false side; only 15-30% of zero-shot false answers become near-hits.
Dead: raising the ceiling with richer candidate lists. A perfect chooser goes from 243 to at most 297 of 552.
Dead: adding more features on top of the encoder's log-probability (the 13-feature model is no better).
Refuted: 'templates are not the cause' as a general statement. It holds only for whole-text similarity; phrase templates drive most Opus false answers.
Refuted: the 70-150x precision gap (corrected to 40-105x), and 'the encoder meets the 2.5e-4 target' (166 vs 165.6, from 1 sampled report).
Refuted: 'drift' as the cause of per-code false-count swings. They are within sampling noise.
Refuted: a composition share of 1/4 in the encoder's 2025-2026 accuracy fall (about 1/3 with finer bins).
Refuted: 'reasoning helps' (31 sampled false for both Opus settings). The reweighted Opus 2025 count of 4,072 understates the natural 6,698.
Refuted: 'every correction reduces to Saerens'. BBSE and sampling-based calibration are separate options.

Weak, rests on 0-2 sampled reports: encoder 166 false (1); Qwen prior-corrected 27/3 (0); enc_and_zs (0); neighbour-hit rule (0); Gemma 74/166 in hindsight (1); the k=3 encoder gate (1-2 extra); the 'clean' results of every strict rule.

Weak, few sampled reports: the gated Opus count of 1,526 (9 sampled, 95% about 670-2,800; the cut was 11x on 2025 but 4.4x on 2026). Opus's yearly false count rests on two template families (10 and 15 sampled, clustered). The SDR figures are reweighted, not natural.
Weak: 'the misses are mostly a label problem' (one reader, 40 items). The audit's endorsement of Opus codes (Opus-family readers, matches their baseline).
